core_loop: gather wood, stone, flax, and other materials -> craft tools and build production structures -> pass discipline tests, many involving other players -> propose petitions and vote on laws -> build monuments -> the Telling ends and the world resets
design_notes: ATITD has no combat; competition runs through seven tests in each discipline, some of which require cooperation, voting, or mass participation, and through player-written law. Seven Monuments built by players who reach Oracle rank end the Telling, after which the world is wiped and the next Telling can change the rules. Discipline tests and periodic world resets are not yet mechanics in the taxonomy (proposal seasonal-world-reset).

mechanics.note: Laws use a controlled variant of Nomic: players write petitions that need a set number of signatures before a vote, and passed laws can restrict options, change ownership, or ban players; an elected Demi-Pharaoh can ban up to seven characters.
The world runs in Tellings that average about a year and a half and end in a full wipe; disciplines with 127 participants can propose a new test for the next Telling.
A Demi-Pharaoh is elected roughly monthly through the Test of the Demi-Pharaoh.
Players gather wood, mine, and harvest flax.
The world runs in Tellings that average about 18 months and end in a full wipe, and what players achieved shapes the rules of the next Telling.

name: A Tale in the Desert
summary: A combat-free MMO set in ancient Egypt in which players gather, craft, and build, pass tests in several disciplines, and govern the world through player-written petitions and votes, with the world wiped and restarted at the end of each Telling.

core_loop: embark with three species and a few goods -> build camps, production, and housing in a cleared glade -> meet each species' needs to keep it content -> complete orders and open glades for reputation -> win before the Queen's impatience fills -> carry rewards to the Smoldering City
design_notes: Against the Storm compresses a city builder into short runs: each settlement is a fresh generated map with a race between two gauges, reputation that the player fills and the Queen's impatience that fills on its own, and earning reputation also lowers impatience. Each village hosts three of seven species with distinct housing, food, luxury, and recreation preferences, so the same production network must serve conflicting demands. Rewards carry over to upgrade the Smoldering City between runs, a meta-progression system the taxonomy lacks (see run proposal).

mechanics.note: The Queen's Impatience gauge fills over time and recalls the player when full; recurring storms raise pressure between calm periods.
Each settlement is won by filling the Reputation gauge through orders, villager contentment, and opened glades.
Production buildings convert goods by recipes such as raincoats, ale, and pies, chosen from a run-specific building set.
Contentment per species responds to met needs; discontented villagers leave and content ones raise reputation.
Seven species with distinct preferences; three per village.
A new map is generated for each settlement across six biomes.
A calm building period alternates with the storm.
Forest glades stay hidden until cut open and may hold boons or threats.
Forest hostility rises as the settlement cuts trees and opens glades.
Meta-progression resources upgrade the Smoldering City between runs.
A visiting trader's wares change each year.

name: Against the Storm
summary: A roguelite city builder in which each settlement must fill a reputation gauge before the Queen's impatience runs out, balancing three villager species' needs while opening dangerous forest glades under a recurring blightstorm.

core_loop: choose a setting -> type a Do, Say, or Story input -> model continues the text from recent story and pinned memory -> player undoes, retries, or edits the output -> next input
design_notes: At runtime the model does all the work: each turn, the game assembles a prompt from the scenario premise, player-pinned memory, and recent story text, and a language model (GPT-2 with 1.5 billion parameters in AI Dungeon 2, GPT-3 through OpenAI's API for the premium Dragon model from July 2020) generates the next passage. There is no separate world state, inventory, or rules engine, so consistency lasts only as long as facts stay in the context window, and undo, retry, and edit are the player's tools for steering. Nick Walton built the first version at a BYU hackathon on a 126-million-parameter GPT-2 and released it in May 2019; Latitude relaunched it in December 2019. It is a boundary case: no system is simulated outside the model's text.

mechanics.note: A language model continues the story text from a prompt of scenario, pinned memory, and recent turns; the See input generates an image that does not change play.
Free-text input typed as Do (action), Say (dialogue), or Story (narration or facts), with blank input asking the model to continue.
Players publish custom adventures and scenarios that others can start from.
Play alternates player input and model output; multiplayer (from April 2020) rotates turns among players' characters while the host can edit model output.

name: AI Dungeon
summary: A text adventure in which a large language model continues the story after each player input, so actions, dialogue, and world facts the player types are improvised into narration rather than resolved by authored rules.

core_loop: visit the island each real day -> gather wood, fruit, fish, bugs, and fossils -> craft D.I.Y. items and spend Bells and Nook Miles -> donate to the museum and decorate -> island rating rises and unlocks services -> new seasons bring new species
design_notes: Time runs on the console clock, and weather, seasons, and species availability follow the hemisphere chosen at start, so a missed month means missing that month's fish and bugs. The developers lowered bank interest and removed waits from landscaping and crafting to reduce the payoff of changing the console clock. The island's one-to-five-star rating gates milestones such as K.K. Slider's concert at three stars, after which the Island Designer lets players add and remove cliffs, water, and paths. The turnip stalk market sells turnips on Sunday mornings, changes buy prices twice daily under one of four weekly patterns, and spoils unsold turnips the next Sunday.

mechanics.note: Game time follows the console clock; days, hemisphere-based seasons, shop hours, and species spawn windows advance while the game is off.
Blathers' museum collects fish, bugs, sea creatures, fossils, and art donated by the player.
D.I.Y. recipes turn gathered wood, stone, iron, fruit, and other materials into tools, furniture, and decorations at a workbench.
Furniture and items can be placed indoors and outdoors anywhere on the island, and the player chooses sites for residents' houses and shops.
The Island Designer edits cliffs, rivers and ponds, and paths.
The island rating (one to five stars) reflects development and scenery; three stars triggers K.K. Slider's concert.
Island growth brings shopkeepers and services such as Nook's Cranny, the museum, and the Able Sisters.
Rocks, fruit, fish, and bugs replenish on daily or multi-day cycles, so gathering is a daily routine.
Turnips bought on Sunday rot the following Sunday while sell prices follow one of four weekly patterns.
Villagers' friendship with the player grows through conversation and gifts.

name: Animal Crossing: New Horizons
summary: A Nintendo life sim on a deserted island whose clock, seasons, and wildlife follow the real calendar, built around gathering, D.I.Y. crafting, museum collections, villager relationships, and island design.

core_loop: settle Latium or Albion and house Liberti -> meet categorized needs with multi-island production chains -> residences advance toward Patricians -> schools produce research and temples belief -> ships carry goods on tracked routes -> defend routes and provinces
design_notes: Anno 117 loosens the strict tier-need ladder: needs fall into categories that can be partly filled, and each good carries attributes with benefits and drawbacks for population, income, health, and satisfaction. Placement matters more than in Anno 1800 because production buildings help or harm nearby structures, paved roads extend building range, and diagonal placement is allowed. Belief tied to chosen gods grants scaling bonuses, a system with no exact taxonomy match (see run proposal).

mechanics.note: Residences advance from Liberti up to Patricians based on access to goods and on nearby prestige or polluting buildings.
Needs are grouped into categories that can be partly fulfilled; each good's attributes add benefits and drawbacks to population, income, health, and satisfaction.
Chains span multiple islands and provinces, linked by warehouses, waystations, and hubs.
Production buildings have positive or negative effects on nearby structures.
Assigned ships carry goods between islands along routes that can be tracked and rerouted.
Schools generate research points for a tree of over 100 unlocks, including repeatable technologies.
Paved roads extend the range and efficiency of structures.
Melee, ranged, and siege units in a rock-paper-scissors system; warships protect routes from pirates.
Ships are modular; adding oars or sails changes how they move.
Standing with the emperor's successor Calidus can earn Consul status or Proconsular authority.

name: Anno 117: Pax Romana
summary: A Roman-era Anno city builder in which residents advance from Liberti to Patricians through categorized needs, buildings affect their neighbors, schools generate research, and modular ships guard multi-island trade.

core_loop: settle an island and house farmers -> meet tier needs with production chains -> houses advance to workers, artisans, engineers, and investors -> higher tiers need goods from other islands and the New World -> build ships and trade routes -> expand under rival pressure
design_notes: Demand is generated by population tiers: basic needs raise how many residents a house holds, luxury needs raise taxes and happiness, and a house advances only when full, supplied, and given construction materials, so each new tier opens a new set of chains. Each tier also staffs its own buildings, so advancing workers to artisans removes labor from worker-tier factories. Old World cities depend on goods from a parallel New World session, so ship routes between sessions are a logistics layer on top of island production.

mechanics.note: Old World tiers Farmers, Workers, Artisans, Engineers, Investors and New World Jornaleros and Obreros; a house advances when full, its basic needs met, and materials available.
Each residence consumes goods per second; basic needs add inhabitants per house, luxury needs add taxes and happiness.
Fixed-recipe buildings chain raw materials into goods; many chains span islands and both sessions.
Ships carry goods between the player's islands, the New World session, and traders.
Trade route ships follow ordered stops with load and unload amounts per good.
Each tier staffs only its tier's production buildings.
Warehouses set island storage limits and pickup range.
AI opponents settle the same map and compete for islands and trade.
Reaching population thresholds of each tier unlocks buildings.
Blueprint mode places silhouettes that are built later with one click when resources exist.
The World's Fair monument is built in stages, each consuming large deliveries of goods, and once complete hosts exhibitions.

name: Anno 1800
summary: An industrial-era city builder in which residents advance through five Old World tiers by consuming goods from multi-island production chains, linked to a New World session by trade routes and contested by AI rivals.

core_loop: load a scenario or join a server -> move and coordinate as infantry or vehicle crew -> spot and engage under ballistics and recoil -> manage load, stamina, and wounds -> complete objectives or die -> build and share new scenarios
design_notes: Arma 3 treats the battlefield as a sandbox: large terrains of up to 163 square kilometers host infantry, vehicles, and aircraft under the same ballistic rules, and scenarios define the war. Much of its life comes from community scenarios and mods built with the Eden editor and SQF scripting, while Bohemia's military consultants reviewed its Tac-Ops missions. Projectile ballistics is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal projectile-ballistics).

mechanics.note: The player is one soldier in first person; clothing and carried equipment add weight that reduces movement speed and stamina.
Infantry, armor, helicopters, jets, and boats share one large terrain, and weapons are heavily affected by external ballistics and recoil, so range and load-out shape every engagement.
The Eden 3D editor and the SQF scripting language let players build single-player and multiplayer scenarios and mods, from realism overhauls to new game modes.
Squad leaders issue orders to AI subordinates.
Scenarios and mods are shared through the Steam Workshop.
Weapons are heavily affected by external ballistics and recoil, so shooters account for drop and travel time at range.

name: Arma 3
summary: A first-person military simulation on large open terrains in which infantry, vehicles, and aircraft fight under modeled ballistics, recoil, and load-based stamina, extended by the Eden editor, SQF scripting, and a large mod community.

core_loop: survey bodies and jump points -> mine Trans-Newtonian minerals and build installations -> research components -> design ship classes -> build fleets and assign officers -> detect and fight with sensors, missiles, and beams -> colonize and expand
design_notes: Aurora began as a helper program for the Starfire board wargame and grew into a standalone simulation with no fixed goals. It exposes almost every subsystem as windows of numbers, from mineral accessibility to officer bonuses and ship maintenance. Time advances in player-chosen steps from 5 seconds to 30 days, so the same engine resolves both strategic expansion and individual missile salvos. The Visual Basic 6 original was superseded by a C# rewrite released in 2020.

mechanics.note: Ship classes are designed from researched components (engines, sensors, weapons, armor), and the player sets armor, speed, and range per class; weapons and sensors must themselves be researched and designed first.
Jump points and mineral deposits stay unknown until gravitational and geological survey sensors sweep each body or survey point, and other ships are known only within sensor detection range.
Eleven Trans-Newtonian Elements sit in finite deposits on planets and asteroids, each with an accessibility rating from 0.1 to 1 that scales mining output; all construction consumes them.
Mines on colonies and asteroid mining extract the minerals.
Research labs are assigned to scientists with field specialties.
Scientists, administrators, naval officers, and ground commanders gain bonuses and improve over time.
Colony cost depends on a world's gravity, atmosphere, and temperature.
Terraforming alters a world's atmosphere to lower its colony cost.
Star systems are randomly generated or built from real star data.
Wealth comes from taxes and exports and is spent on construction, research, and maintenance.
Ships require maintenance support, which can be disabled in setup.
The player chooses each time increment, from 5 seconds to 30 days, and the engine resolves movement, detection, combat, and production for it.
Star systems can be built from real star data instead of generated at random.

name: Aurora 4X
summary: A free space 4X simulation by a single developer in which the player runs an interstellar empire through ship design from components, mineral mining, sensor-based detection, missile and beam combat, and named officers, with time advanced in steps from seconds to days.

claims.text: A public demo was released on itch.io on 2017-07-05 and the full PC game on Steam on 2019-10-17; `year` records the 2019 release rather than the demo. Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One versions released on 2022-06-16.

core_loop: gather sticks and stone by hand -> craft tools and a workerbot -> teach the bot a task by demonstrating it -> edit the visual script into a loop -> chain bots into farming, crafting, and cooking lines -> supply Folk with food, housing, and care -> unlock new buildings and bot parts
design_notes: Autonauts, from Denki and designers Gary Penn and Aaron Puzey, makes automation a matter of teaching: the player performs an action while a bot watches, the bot records it as blocks in a Scratch-style visual language, and the player adds repeat loops and conditions so the routine runs unattended. Programs are bounded by bot hardware: the head sets maximum instructions (12 at Mk 0 to 32 at Mk 3, raised by brain upgrades) and search range, the body sets hand, backpack, and upgrade slots, and the drive sets speed, battery, and recharge time, so better routines need better-built bots. Folk are the demand side, consuming food that lasts from 10 seconds for water to 120 seconds for apple pie or cooked fish and needing housing and baths, and they are either fully happy or unhappy. Colonise mode introduces components step by step, while Free and Creative modes unlock everything.

mechanics.note: Bots learn a task by recording the player's demonstrated actions as Scratch-style blocks that the player edits into loops and conditions; the bot's head caps the number of instructions at 12 to 32 plus brain upgrades.

Bots are built from a head, body, and drive at Mk 0 to Mk 3 that set instruction limit and search range, hand and backpack slots, and speed, battery, and recharge time, with upgrade slots for brain, sensor, speed, and energy parts.
Workbenches and crafting stations turn crops, clay, wood, and other materials into tools, pottery, baked food, and clothing through multi-step recipes that bots run in chains.
Housed Folk consume food whose satiation lasts from 10 seconds (water) to 120 seconds (apple pie, cooked fish) and need baths after messy meals; each Folk is either fully happy or unhappy.
The Autonaut harvests sticks and stone and crafts the first tools, workbenches, and bot parts from blueprints before bots take over.
Bots plant, grow, and harvest crops that feed cooking chains.
Animal husbandry and fishing supply food and materials alongside farming.
Research unlocks new buildings, recipes, and bot parts, and bots can be programmed to do science.
The player's Autonaut walks the map, carries items, and performs each task once so bots can learn it.
Players share Automods, including bots and scripts, on Steam Workshop.
A bot's head caps its program at 12 to 32 instructions, raised by brain upgrades, so longer routines need better-built bots.
Bots watch the player perform a task and record it as Scratch-style blocks, which the player edits into loops and conditions; this teaching step is the game's main interface to automation.

name: Autonauts
summary: A colony automation game in which the player crafts workerbots from parts and teaches them farming, crafting, and cooking routines in a Scratch-style visual language, so that bots supply the food, housing, and care that a growing population of Folk needs.

core_loop: review the world map and country data -> commit aid, treaties, and interventions -> rival superpower responds -> contested moves become crises -> escalate or back down -> prestige shifts -> next annual turn
design_notes: Crawford built the game around country-level state (alignment, government stability, insurgency) that responds to superpower actions, and around a two-sided crisis exchange in which backing down costs prestige and pushing too far ends the game in nuclear war. Ending the game at nuclear war, rather than letting the war be fought, is its main difference from Bruce Ketchledge's Geopolitique 1990. The crisis escalation exchange is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal crisis-escalation).

mechanics.note: Each turn the player allocates economic and military aid, support for governments or insurgents, interventions, and treaties to minor countries to pull their alignment; the AI superpower answers, and contested moves become crises resolved by no action, diplomatic notes, or military maneuvers.

Prestige points are the score: winning crises and holding aligned countries raises prestige, backing down in a crisis costs prestige and has political repercussions, and the total after eight years decides the outcome.
Eight one-year turns; each turn resolves both superpowers' policies and then presents the year's incidents as crises to settle before advancing.
Minor-country governments face insurgencies whose strength shifts with superpower aid to the government or the rebels.
Incidents and crises arrive framed as newspaper stories.
The world map can be shaded by country-level variables such as alignment and insurgency.

name: Balance of Power
summary: A Cold War geopolitical sim in which the player, as US or Soviet leader, spends aid, treaties, and interventions on minor countries over eight annual turns and manages escalating crises to gain prestige without triggering nuclear war.

claims.text: Banished is credited with starting the survival city-builder trend.

core_loop: assign citizens to gathering, farming, and building jobs -> stockpile food, firewood, and tools for winter -> families form when housing exists and children grow into workers -> aging, disease, and disasters remove citizens -> expand or collapse
design_notes: Citizens are the main resource: every worker is a person who was born, ages, needs a house to start a family, and dies, so the town's age structure produces labor booms and busts years after a decision. There is no money and no tech tree; any building is available once its resources exist, and trade is barter with visiting ships that can also bring disease. Designer Luke Hodorowicz cited the Anno series as a big inspiration and left combat out, and the genre literature credits Banished with starting the survival city-builder trend.

mechanics.note: Residents are born, age, work, start families, and die; age cohorts create delayed labor shortages.
Crops are planted and harvested on an annual cycle, and winter demands stored food and firewood.
Each household consumes food, firewood, clothing, and tools; shortages lead to cold, illness, and starvation.
The player sets worker counts per workplace and profession; unassigned citizens become laborers.
Laborers carry resources to stockpiles and construction sites, so their number sets delivery speed.
Foresters cut and replant forests; land used for forests or quarries cannot hold housing.
Trade ships can bring illness from abroad.
Resources are bartered with trade vessels at a trading post; there is no currency.
Fires and tornadoes destroy buildings.
Couples need an empty house to start a family and have children.
Nomad groups can arrive and ask to join the town.

name: Banished
summary: A survival city builder without money or a tech tree in which exiled families gather, farm, and stockpile for winter while aging, births, disease, and disasters decide whether the town grows or starves.

claims.text: A free tech demo and paid alpha launched on 2013-08-03 through FastSpring, before Steam Early Access on 2015-05-29; the source reports no 1.0 release.

core_loop: pick a vehicle and map -> drive, race, or stage a crash -> node-beam structure deforms and parts fail -> inspect the damage -> reset or change vehicle, conditions, or mods
design_notes: Vehicles are defined in JBeam, a JSON format of nodes and beams, and the same structure produces both handling and damage: frames flex, doors detach, windows shatter, tires blow, engines degrade, and fuel tanks can explode. Free roam exposes simulation parameters (time, gravity, wind), so much play is experiment rather than goal. Lua scripting and an official in-game mod repository make the vehicle and scenario set community-driven, and BeamNG.tech forks the engine for education and research.

mechanics.note: Vehicles are JBeam node-and-beam skeletons that flex and deform under impact; damage degrades engines, detaches doors, shatters windows, blows tires, and can make fuel tanks explode.
Handling comes from the same node-beam structure, so suspension, chassis flex, and tires respond to the vehicle's build and its damage.
Campaigns group short races, chases, and stunts, and time trials race against the player's best times.
The game relies heavily on Lua, and mods add real and fictional vehicles.
An official mod repository is browsable from the website and in game, with a manager that keeps mods updated.

name: BeamNG.drive
summary: A vehicle sim built on soft-body physics in which every vehicle is a node-and-beam skeleton that flexes, deforms, and breaks under impact, played as a free-roam sandbox with scenarios.

core_loop: read the level objective -> attach blocks, wheels, hinges, and weapons to a starting block -> bind controls -> run the level and drive the machine -> watch it work, flip, or break apart -> revise the design
design_notes: Machines grow from a single starting block, and each attached block is a rigid body joined to its neighbor by a breakable joint; powered wheels, hinges, pistons, and springs are bound to player keys, so a machine is both a structure and a control scheme. Designs fail by tipping, tearing at weak joints, or setting themselves alight, which is much of the appeal. Logic blocks (timers, logic gates, sensors) added later let machines act without input, and the level editor and PC multiplayer turned designs into contests.

mechanics.note: Machines are built outward from a starting block using 70+ blocks such as wooden blocks, powered wheels, hinges, pistons, cannons, bombs, flamethrowers, and balloons; block placement sets mass distribution and what each key does.
Each block is a physics body connected by joints that break under excess force, so machines buckle, tip, or tear apart while driving and fighting.
55 campaign levels across four islands set goals such as destroying buildings, defeating troops, or solving puzzles with magical artifacts.
The player drives the finished machine in real time with keys bound to its powered parts.
Fire spreads across wooden blocks and enemy buildings; bombs and cannons break blocks.
Timers, logic gates, and proximity sensors simulate key presses so machines can automate sequences.
Machines and levels are shared on Steam Workshop.
An in-game modloader supports community mods with new blocks and logic.

name: Besiege
summary: A physics construction game where the player builds medieval siege machines from blocks, wheels, and weapons, then drives them against castles and armies in objective levels or a sandbox.

core_loop: rent a building and renovate it -> buy stock and set prices -> customers visit and buy -> hire staff and managers -> import from the harbour into warehouses -> trucks deliver to stores -> invest profits in more businesses and real estate
design_notes: Big Ambitions starts the business at street level: the avatar personally rents, furnishes, stocks, and runs the first store and must also eat, sleep, and stay healthy and happy. Growth comes from replacing the player's own labor with staff and then with managers (HR managers, logistics managers, purchasing agents) who automate hiring, purchasing, and delivery from an HQ. Supply moves through a physical chain from harbour importers to warehouses to stores on delivery trucks. Business types range from gift shops and supermarkets to law firms and web development.

mechanics.note: The player walks and drives through New York City to rent buildings, buy stock, restock shelves, and run errands until staff take over.
Customers decide whether to buy based on the store's prices and the products and service it offers.
Employees are hired with skills and wages for each business, then HR managers, logistics managers, and purchasing agents automate operations from an HQ.
Rented buildings are renovated and furnished with shelves, registers, and fixtures that set what a store can sell and how many customers it serves.
Stock fills store shelves and warehouses; empty shelves lose sales.
Delivery trucks carry goods from harbour importers to warehouses and stores.
Managers at the HQ take over hiring, purchasing, and logistics.
The avatar must eat food stored at home, sleep, and stay healthy and happy.
Bank loans fund early expansion.
Businesses keep opening hours and staff work scheduled shifts.
Paid marketing campaigns raise customer traffic to the player's businesses.

name: Big Ambitions
summary: A business life sim set in a simulated New York City in which the player's avatar rents storefronts, stocks and staffs shops, builds warehouse logistics, and grows from one store into a business empire.

core_loop: import an ingredient -> route it through machines that change its concentration -> activate cures and remove side effects -> form pills and ship them -> grade and price against market demand and rivals -> research better machines
design_notes: Big Pharma's production puzzle is numeric: each ingredient carries cures and side effects that are active only inside concentration windows on a 0 to 20 scale, and machines raise, lower, combine, or transform effects at set concentrations. A line is a sequence of machines on conveyor belts in a fixed floor plan, so the order of operations and the space they take are both constraints. Products are graded from effectiveness, side effects, and market demand, and rival companies release competing drugs that saturate a disease's market. The primary challenge is line layout rather than corporate strategy, which places it in the factory-automation lineage with a business layer.

mechanics.note: Machines raise or lower an ingredient's concentration, combine materials, or transform effects; each effect is active only inside its concentration window on a 0 to 20 scale.
Conveyor belts move materials between machines from intake ports to output ports, and machine order along the belt sets the recipe.
Each finished drug gets a letter grade from its cure strength, side effects, and market demand, and the player names and prices it.
Rival companies release competing drugs that saturate a disease's market and cut demand for the player's product.
Price and sales for each cure depend on demand and how crowded its market is.
Machines are placed on a fixed factory floor where space limits line length.
A research tree unlocks better machines and other benefits.
Explorers search for new ingredients, and analysis machines reveal an ingredient's effects and maximum potency.
Scenarios set targets such as a financial milestone within a set number of years, at several difficulties.

name: Big Pharma
summary: A pharmaceutical factory and business sim in which the player routes ingredients through machines on conveyor belts to push their concentration into the range that activates cures while suppressing side effects, then sells into contested markets.

claims.text: The earliest dated changelog entry is v0.26.4 on 2017-08-01 and earlier versions are undated, so the 2017 first public web release is inferred; version 1.0.0 is dated 2021-11-10 and the Steam release was 2021-12-10.
Bitburner was started by danielyxie and is now developed as open source by hundreds of contributors, with the Steam release credited to Fulcrum Games, hydroflame, and GitHub contributors.
Its listed inspirations are Else Heart.break(), Hacknet, Uplink, and Deus Ex, none of which are in this dataset.

core_loop: write a script -> gain root on servers -> run hack, grow, and weaken threads -> earn money and hacking experience -> buy RAM and programs -> gain faction reputation -> buy augmentations and install them, resetting progress -> destroy a BitNode for a Source-File and start the next
design_notes: Bitburner is an incremental game whose economy is a small numerical model the player automates in code. Each server holds a money stock and a security level: hack() steals a percentage of the money and raises security, grow() multiplies money back and also raises security, and weaken() lowers security toward a floor of max(1, round(starting security / 3)), with hack chance and timing set by security and the player's hacking level. Writing schedulers that balance these three calls across many servers and threads is the main skill. Progress is layered by resets: augmentations bought with money and faction reputation (each purchase doubling later prices) take effect only when installed, which wipes most progress, and destroying a BitNode by hacking w0r1d_d43m0n at hacking level 3000 resets further but grants a permanent Source-File. This prestige-reset structure has no taxonomy entry, so this run proposed one. Later BitNodes add systems such as Bladeburner and sleeves.

mechanics.note: Netscript scripts in JavaScript run on servers whose RAM caps how many threads can run; the TIX API automates stock trading, and a beginner path teaches programming from scratch.

hack() takes a share of a server's finite money that rises with hacking level and falls with security; grow() restores money and weaken() lowers security toward its floor, and both hack and grow raise security, so sustained yield needs a balanced hack-grow-weaken schedule.
Working for factions builds reputation that gates which augmentations can be bought; Daedalus reputation gates The Red Pill needed to end a BitNode.
Hacking, combat, and charisma stats rise with use; hacking level raises success chance and money stolen, shortens hack time, and gates which servers can be hacked.
Stock prices move about every 6 seconds by a forecast probability that large trades shift; hacking or growing a company's server can lower or raise its stock's hidden forecast.
Coding contracts found on servers pose programming problems that earn rewards when solved.
Time spent offline accumulates and later speeds stock-market updates from about every 6 seconds to about every 4.
Each script has a RAM cost, and a server's RAM caps how many script threads can run on it, so buying RAM and writing lean scripts both raise income.

name: Bitburner
summary: A free, open-source incremental hacking game in which the player writes JavaScript scripts that hack, grow, and weaken simulated servers for money, then spends it with faction reputation on augmentations that reset progress in exchange for permanent multipliers.

core_loop: impress villagers with miracles, help, or fear -> belief grows and worship generates prayer power -> cast miracles with the Hand and gestures -> train the creature with strokes and slaps -> the creature acts on learned desires -> convert rival villages and move to the next island
design_notes: Richard Evans built the creature on a belief-desire-intention model after Bratman: beliefs are lists of data about world objects, desires are simplified perceptrons, and opinions are decision trees about how to satisfy a desire; the creature picks the belief with the best opinion for each desire as its intention, and strokes and slaps adjust those opinions by reinforcement. A leash directs the creature's attention so it can learn by observation. The player's actions also move a good-evil alignment that changes the land, interface, music, and followers' view of the god, with a good and an evil advisor arguing each case; alignment has no mechanic id yet (proposal filed). The interface is an animated hand that throws objects and casts gestures instead of icons and panels.

mechanics.note: The creature forms intentions from a belief-desire-intention model with perceptron desires and decision-tree opinions; stroking rewards and slapping discourages the last action, the creature remembers and generalizes these responses, and a leash focuses it on actions the player demonstrates.

Miracles such as food, wood, healing, shields, fireballs, and lightning are cast from the Temple or Village Centre or by drawing gestures with the Hand, powered by villagers' worship, sacrifices, or one-shot Miracle Dispensers.
Each villager holds a belief level in the player's god, raised by help or intimidation; villagers tire of repeated tactics, and a village converts when enough believe.
The creature must be fed and taught what and when to eat, and it grows over the game.
Villagers need food, healing, and rest before they will worship.
A good and an evil advisor push the player toward each alignment.
Buildings are placed from Workshop blueprints and built by villagers.
Villagers gather wood and food, for example by fishing.
Real local weather can be imported.

name: Black & White
summary: A god game in which the player wins villagers' belief through miracles, help, or fear while training a giant creature whose behavior is learned from the player's rewards and punishments.

core_loop: place housing plots and roads -> walkers from service buildings roam the roads and cover the houses they pass -> houses evolve when food, goods, and services reach them -> taxes and trade fund the city -> raise culture, prosperity, peace, and favor ratings to win the mission
design_notes: Coverage is delivered by individual walkers whose routes depend on road layout, so the same buildings serve a block well or badly depending on junctions; the developers cited SimCity's static placement as what they wanted to make less static. In the logic preserved by the Julius re-implementation, a walker sets a house's coverage to 96 and coverage decays by 1 per update, while prefects zero fire risk and engineers zero collapse risk. City and empire share one map, and gods that punish neglect have no matching taxonomy mechanic (see run proposal).

mechanics.note: Service walkers leave their building and roam roads; each house passed gets coverage set to 96, which decays by 1 per update until the next visit.
Housing evolves through levels from tents up to villas and palaces when food, goods, services, and desirability are met, and devolves when they lapse.
Each assignment sets population and thresholds for four ratings: culture, prosperity, peace, and favor.
Higher houses need food plus pottery, furniture, oil, and wine delivered by market walkers.
Raw materials such as clay, olives, and timber become pottery, oil, and furniture in workshops.
An empire map opens land and sea routes to cities that buy and sell specific goods.
Buildings accumulate fire and collapse risk that prefects and engineers reset to zero.
Favor with Caesar rises with timely tribute and gifts and falls when requests are missed.
Military assignments bring invasions; legions, walls, and towers defend the city map.
Buildings need workers from housing; shortages idle walkers and industry.
Gardens, statues, and plazas raise desirability that houses need to evolve.
Walkers and goods move on roads, so road layout sets coverage.

name: Caesar III
summary: A Roman city builder in which service walkers roam the roads from their buildings, houses evolve only where food, goods, and services actually reach them, and missions are won on culture, prosperity, peace, and favor ratings.

core_loop: buy land and place a firm -> lay out its internal units -> link purchasing, manufacturing, and sales units into supply chains -> set prices and advertising -> compete for market share on price, quality, and brand -> reinvest, research, or trade stock
design_notes: Trevor Chan's Capitalism models a firm as a small grid of internal units (purchasing, manufacturing, sales, advertising) that the player wires together, so every factory, farm, mine, and store is a layout and logistics puzzle inside a market model. Retail is the main income source: each department store sells up to four products, and customers weigh price, product quality, and brand against competing stores. R&D centers raise product quality over projects lasting from six months to ten years, and AI rivals can be set from aggressive to conservative. An optional stock market allows takeovers, and hired presidents can run divisions. Advertising spend that builds brand awareness has no mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as advertising-awareness).

mechanics.note: Factories turn purchased inputs into products through linked manufacturing units; farms, mines, oil wells, and logging camps supply raw materials.
City consumers pick among stores by price, product quality, and brand; each department store stocks up to four items.
AI corporations with aggressive to conservative management styles compete in the same cities for market share.
Each firm is a grid of internal units placed and linked by the player; layout decides what flows where.
Product quality comes from input quality and technology level and drives demand and price.
R&D centers run projects from six months to ten years that raise technology and unlock new products.
An optional stock market lets the player buy shares, take over rivals, or be bought out.
Mines, oil wells, farms, and logging camps produce raw materials.
Hired presidents can run divisions day to day.
A layout plan library saves and reuses firm unit layouts.
Seventeen scenarios set goals such as market-share dominance within a time limit.
Advertising units inside firms spend money to raise a product's brand rating, which customers weigh with price and quality when choosing among stores.

name: Capitalism
summary: A corporate business sim in which the player builds retail stores, factories, farms, mines, and R&D centers from internal unit layouts and competes with AI firms on price, quality, and brand across city markets.

claims.text: Captain of Industry entered Steam Early Access on 2022-05-31 and was still in Early Access in October 2026, with the developers estimating two to four more years.

core_loop: designate mining and dumping areas -> trucks haul ore and rock -> smelt and refine into goods -> feed, power, and house the population -> satisfied needs generate Unity -> spend Unity and products on research, edicts, and ship expeditions -> expand and terraform
design_notes: Captain of Industry joins a factory game to a settlement whose population is both labor and a consumer: residents need housing, food, water, electricity, healthcare, and household goods, each fully satisfied need yields about one to two Unity per month, and Unity buys edicts, outposts, quick trades, instant construction, and emergency repairs. Every working vehicle and many buildings consume crafted Maintenance I, II, or III; below 75% a monthly breakdown roll begins, reaching 50% at zero, so maintenance is itself a production chain whose failure cascades through the economy. Terrain is a stock of materials: excavators dig inside a Mine Control Tower's area, trucks dump rock and dirt that settle at per-material angles of repose (about 42 degrees for loose dirt to 78 for hardened rock), and dumping reclaims ocean for ports. A ship explores a world map for islands, refugees, and trade partners. Unity works like a political-capital currency earned from welfare, which the taxonomy lacks; this run proposed one.

mechanics.note: Smelters, refineries, chemical plants, food processors, and assembly lines run recipe chains from iron and copper ore to electronics, fuel, consumer goods, and nuclear fuel across 100+ technologies.
Trucks are assigned to mines, storages, and buildings and automatically deliver products where they are needed, so fleet size and road layout cap throughput before belts and trains replace them.

Mining designations inside a Mine Control Tower area lower terrain and dumping designations raise it; loose material settles at per-material angles of repose, retaining walls stabilize slopes, and dumping can reclaim ocean.
Residents consume food, water, electricity, healthcare, and household goods; each fully satisfied need yields Unity, and unmet food or health shrinks the population.
Working vehicles and buildings consume Maintenance I to III crafted at depots (idle at about a third); below 75% maintenance a breakdown is rolled monthly with chance rising to 50% at zero.
Excavators dig ore, coal, limestone, and rock from designated terrain, while oil rigs, quartz and uranium mines, and water pumps work fixed deposits and outposts.
The player paints mining and dumping designations, and excavators and trucks assigned to a Mine Control Tower carry out the work inside its area.
Belts and pipes give high-throughput direct links between machines once truck logistics become a bottleneck.
Generators up to nuclear reactors feed the settlement and factories, and residents require electricity as one of their needs.
Research labs consume products and Unity to unlock over 100 technologies from basic smelting to space flight.
Air and water pollution and unmanaged waste spread disease among the population.
Production emits slag, waste, carbon dioxide, wastewater, and spent nuclear fuel that must be dumped, treated, recycled, or stored.
Captain's Office edicts change settlement rules, such as raising population growth by tier, for a monthly Unity cost.
Ships explore a world map to discover islands and trading partners; quick trades and recurring contracts exchange goods.
Farms grow crops for food and industrial inputs, fertilizer boosts yields, and greenhouses grow advanced crops.
Storages and loose storage piles buffer materials, and full outputs stall production upstream.
Trains move bulk cargo over long distances, and ships run trade contracts between the home island and partners.
Unity income, population change, edict costs, and maintenance breakdown rolls resolve monthly.
Each fully satisfied settlement need yields about 1 to 2 Unity per month, spent on edicts, outposts, quick trades, instant construction, and emergency repairs.
Unity is spent on building boosts (0.25 Unity each) that speed up individual buildings.

name: Captain of Industry
summary: An industrial colony builder in which the player reshapes island terrain with excavators and trucks, runs production chains to feed, house, and power a settlement, and spends the Unity its satisfied population generates on edicts, quick builds, and world-map expansion.

core_loop: accept a generated customer order -> inspect and test the car -> remove parts in order to reach faulty ones -> buy or repair replacements -> reassemble and test drive -> get paid -> upgrade the garage and restore cars for sale
design_notes: The car is a tree of modeled parts (over 4000 across 72 cars) with a removal order, so labor is spent reaching a faulty component before replacing it, the series loop carried over from Car Mechanic Simulator 2018. Customer orders are generated without end, while story missions, car and salvage auctions, barn finds, and a project-car restoration supply variety. A skills and garage-upgrade system gates faster or more capable work.

mechanics.note: Orders list symptoms; the player examines engine, suspension, and chassis, removes covering parts in a realistic order to reach damaged ones, replaces or repairs them, and verifies the fix, across over 4000 parts on 72 cars.
An endless supply of generated customer orders plus story missions with their own requirements provide income.
Car auctions and salvage auctions supply restoration projects for resale.
Experience feeds a skills and garage-upgrade system.
Repaired and tuned cars can be driven, including time trials on a race track.

name: Car Mechanic Simulator 2021
summary: A first-person garage sim in which the player diagnoses and repairs customer cars part by part, restores auction and barn-find cars, and expands the workshop.

claims.text: Early access began 2015-07-15 and 1.0 released 2024-12-05, published by Kitfox Games.
Caves of Qud is among the shipped games listed as using wave function collapse.

core_loop: explore generated and handmade zones -> fight, trade, and talk with faction members -> mutate and equip -> uncover generated history -> go deeper
design_notes: A roguelike included for its simulation layers: faction reputation that every creature carries, liquids that mix and flow, body-part anatomy, and procedurally generated sultan histories that the world refers to. It is a frequently cited example of wave function collapse in a shipped game.

mechanics.note: Every creature belongs to factions; the player's standing with each faction decides who attacks, trades, or talks.
Generated histories of past sultans are written into the world as lore, shrines, and quests.
Zones mix handmade and procedural maps; some generators use wave function collapse.

name: Caves of Qud
summary: A science-fantasy roguelike RPG with simulated factions, liquids, body parts, and procedurally generated histories, built partly with wave function collapse.

claims.text: Cities: Skylines is credited with reviving the SimCity style of city builder after SimCity (2013).

core_loop: draw roads and zone along them -> citizens move in, commute, and shop along computed routes -> population milestones unlock services and map tiles -> set district policies, taxes, and budgets -> fix traffic with road hierarchy and transit -> expand
design_notes: Colossal Order carried the road and transit systems of its Cities in Motion series into a full city builder, so every citizen and vehicle is an agent taking the fastest route and congestion is read directly from visible jams. Zoning cells are generated along whatever road geometry the player draws, freeing layouts from a fixed grid, and districts let the player apply policies and tax rates to painted areas. Paradox approved the project after the reception of SimCity (2013), the game was built for Steam Workshop mods, and widely used mods replace core systems such as traffic rules.

mechanics.note: Zoning cells follow the shape of drawn roads; residential, commercial, industrial, and office zones develop and level up.
Road type sets lanes, speed, and zone frontage; network geometry such as interchanges and one-way systems decides throughput.
Each citizen takes the fastest route to work or other destinations; poor road design shows up as visible jams that delay services and deliveries.
Player-drawn bus, tram, train, metro, ferry, and taxi lines carry passengers, cut congestion, and earn fares.
Citizens and vehicles path individually through roads, paths, and transit.
Population milestones unlock services, zoning types, policies, and purchase of up to 25 map tiles.
District policies restrict development types, set district tax rates, or make transit free.
Water and sewage pipes; sewage released upstream contaminates downstream intakes.
Service buildings reach buildings by network distance and dispatch vehicles.
Elementary (300), high school (1,000), and university (4,500) capacities move citizens through four education levels that higher-level jobs require.
Citizens age and die; an initial cohort moving in together can age into a wave of deaths that overloads hearses.
Services and parks raise land value, pollution and noise lower it, and land value helps buildings level up.
Steam Workshop and a mod-friendly architecture; mods add assets, maps, and new behavior.
Citizens choose between walking, driving, and the player's bus, tram, train, metro, ferry, and taxi lines when routing to destinations, so new lines shift demand off roads.

name: Cities: Skylines
summary: A city builder in which road-following zones, agent citizens who route to work along computed paths, district policies, and player-drawn transit lines make traffic flow the central design problem.

core_loop: zone and draw roads -> citizens choose homes, jobs, and routes by cost, time, and comfort -> taxes and fees fund services -> milestones grant development points and map tiles -> unlock transport and services -> expand
design_notes: Route choice is a weighted cost over time, comfort, money, and behavior, so parking fees, transit fares, and lane choice shift where agents go, and the first game's cap of about 65,000 rendered citizens is replaced by a hardware limit. One in-game day and night stands for a month, so daily traffic rhythms and seasonal climate run on different scales. The launch drew criticism for performance and its economy simulation, console versions were delayed indefinitely in 2024, and development moved from Colossal Order to Iceflake Studios after a November 2025 announcement.

mechanics.note: Residential, commercial, industrial, and office zones along roads, with signature buildings unlocked at milestones.
Vehicles spread across lanes, parking fees enter route cost, and accident checks run per road segment.
Citizens compare driving, transit, and walking with a cost combining time, comfort, money, and personal preference.
Development points are spent in a tree to unlock transport options and services.
Milestones grant development points and map tiles, from 9 starting tiles up to 441.
Each map has a preset climate; winters bring snow.
Floods, forest fires, and tornadoes, mitigated by disaster response services.
Each day and night cycle equals one simulated month.
Signature buildings and services change land value in their zone.
Tax rates, fees, and ordinances fund the city.
Paradox Mods since 2024-03-25; mods can override game code.
Citizens compare driving, transit, and walking using a cost of time, comfort, money, and personal behavior, and parking fees enter the driving cost.
Generation, a connected grid, and batteries; solar output varies with weather and time of day and wind with wind strength.
Weather and seasons affect solar and wind output and climate conditions.

name: Cities: Skylines II
summary: The sequel to Cities: Skylines, with citizens choosing routes by time, comfort, and money, a tech tree of development points, preset climates with seasons, and maps of up to 441 tiles.

core_loop: explore with units -> found and grow cities -> allocate production and research -> unlock advances and wonders -> expand, trade, or fight rivals -> win by conquest or the space race
design_notes: Meier and Shelley combined the technology tree of Francis Tresham's board game with Empire's exploration and conquest and Railroad Tycoon's idea of several interacting systems managed at once; a SimCity-style zoning layer in an early prototype was dropped. Each city works surrounding terrain tiles for food, production, and trade, a worked-tile yield model the taxonomy does not yet name (proposal worked-tile-yields), and battles resolve from unit attack and defense values (proposal stat-combat-resolution). Wonders exist once per world, so building one denies it to every rival.

mechanics.note: Advances are researched one at a time through a prerequisite graph adapted from Tresham's 1980 board game, from Pottery and the Wheel to Nuclear Fission and Space Flight; each unlocks units, city improvements, wonders, or governments, so research order shapes the game.
Turns run from 4000 BC to as late as AD 2100; each turn every city produces and every unit moves, against two to seven AI civilizations.
The map starts hidden and is revealed by exploring units; barbarians emerge from huts, unclaimed land, and the sea, and become rarer as exploration proceeds.
Relations with rival civilizations lead to alliances, peace, or war.
Government forms unlocked by research change the economic and military rules of the civilization.
The player sets tax rates and the share of trade spent on research.
Cities track content and unhappy citizens; luxuries, temples, and wonders keep cities out of civil disorder.
Settlers build roads and later railroads that speed movement between cities.
Random worlds are generated for each game, with an alternative Earth map.
Corruption removes part of each city's trade, rising with distance from the Palace and depending on government type; a Courthouse reduces it.
Cities are captured by moving a military unit into them, transferring the city and its worked tiles to the conqueror.
Combat compares the attacker's attack value with the defender's defense under terrain and fortification modifiers and a random draw, and the loser is destroyed.

name: Sid Meier's Civilization
summary: A turn-based 4X game in which the player guides a civilization from 4000 BC toward the space age by founding cities, researching a technology tree, building one-per-world wonders, and competing with rival civilizations by diplomacy or war.

core_loop: read the scenario briefing -> set doctrine, emissions control, and weapon release authority -> assign units to patrol, strike, and support missions -> sensors detect and classify contacts -> weapons engage under doctrine -> adjust missions as detections and losses accrue
design_notes: CMO simulates the sensor and weapon chain rather than abstract unit strengths: detection depends on radar propagation, terrain, thermal layers, and weather, and engagement depends on database specifications and doctrine. The player works mostly at mission and doctrine level and lets tactical AI fly and fight, so one player can run scenarios from patrol-boat skirmishes to global war. The Command engine also has a Professional Edition with full database editing, umpire-controlled multiplayer, and Monte Carlo analysis, sold to defense organizations.

mechanics.note: Every platform's sensors and weapons come from a database of tens of thousands of real systems; radar propagation, sensor degradation, terrain masking, sonar thermal layers, weather, jamming, and anti-radiation strikes are modeled for thousands of active platforms in real time.
Each side sees only what its sensors detect; emission control (EMCON) policies trade a unit's own detection range against revealing it to enemy passive sensors.
Units are assigned to patrol, strike, and support missions and executed by tactical AI under doctrine settings such as weapon release authority and EMCON.
Contacts begin unidentified and are classified as sensor data accumulates.
Direct orders override a unit's mission behavior.
Scenarios lasting hours to days of game time run with time acceleration and pause.
Over 600 official and community scenarios plus a quick battle generator.
A Lua scripting engine and scenario editor let players build custom operations.
Scenarios are shared through the Steam Workshop.
Weather degrades sensors and affects engagements.
Ballistics are among the modeled effects alongside sensor propagation, so weapon flight and impact follow database specifications.

name: Command: Modern Operations
summary: A real-time operational military simulation in which the player commands air, naval, and land units drawn from a database of tens of thousands of real platforms, sensors, and weapons on a map of Earth, managing doctrine, emissions control, and missions.

core_loop: check documents -> search the vehicle with UV light and tools -> extract contraband or approve -> arrest or chase fleeing smugglers -> earn cash -> upgrade the post, cars, and defenses -> story missions and raids
design_notes: It moves the Papers, Please inspection loop into a 3D first-person space: document discrepancies are found on paper, but contraband is found physically by examining the vehicle with a UV flashlight and extracting it with tools. The number of documents per entrant grows over time, raising the error rate at constant attention. Inspection income funds post upgrades whose maintenance costs rise, while authored special assignments, chases, and gang raids interrupt the shift loop.

mechanics.note: Drivers present documents whose number grows over the campaign; small discrepancies require refusal, and suspicious vehicles are searched with a UV flashlight before tools extract hidden goods.
The player walks the post in first person, opens and searches vehicles, drives upgradable police cars in pursuits, and uses firearms in shootouts.
Cash from inspections, foiled smuggling, and interventions pays for upgrades while post maintenance costs rise over time.
Gang attacks on the post are countered with purchased defense upgrades.
Special assignments and story decisions shape the fate of Acaristan and lead to multiple endings.

name: Contraband Police
summary: A first-person border-post sim set in 1981 in which the player checks drivers' documents, searches vehicles for hidden contraband, chases smugglers, and upgrades the post against gang attacks.

claims.text: Norn genetics are haploid, with no dominant or recessive genes and no recombination between loci, and mutation can disable organs or produce Norns that cannot see or hear.

core_loop: hatch eggs -> Norns act on biochemical drives -> player rewards, punishes, and teaches words -> neural weights shift toward drive-reducing actions -> Norns breed and pass mutated genomes -> next generation behaves differently
design_notes: Steve Grand built each Norn as a stack of coupled models rather than a scripted pet: a neural network whose sight neurons are grouped one per object type, a biochemistry of chemicals and organs that sets drive levels, and a haploid genome with no dominance that codes for both. Learning is behaviorist: high drive levels act as punishment and reductions as reward, so the player's tickles and slaps only matter through the same chemistry. Because the genome builds the brain and body, mutations produce Norns that cannot see, lack organs, or never die, which the online breeding community catalogued and traded. Norns live about 40 hours, short enough for many generations.

mechanics.note: A neural-network brain maps sensed objects and drives to actions; drive reduction reinforces the action that preceded it, and the hand's tickle and slap act as reward and punishment through the same pathway.
Haploid digital genomes with no dominant or recessive genes encode brain wiring, biochemistry, and organs; offspring genomes mutate, and every boxed copy shipped a unique starting set of egg genomes.
Drives such as hunger and tiredness are concentrations in a simulated biochemistry that rise over time and fall when actions such as eating or resting succeed.
The player's hand pointer feeds Norns, shows them objects, and tickles or slaps them; neglect leads to hunger, disease, and death, but care shapes behavior only indirectly through learning.
Players teach nouns by naming objects a Norn is looking at and verbs with a learning computer, then type instructions that the Norn may choose to obey.
Norns hatch, grow, breed, and die within roughly 40 hours of play.
Grendels steal food, injure Norns, and carry diseases that sicken the population.
Exported Norns and genomes were swapped and bred across players by a large online community.

name: Creatures
summary: An artificial-life game in which the player hatches and raises Norns whose neural-network brains, simulated biochemistry, and haploid digital genomes produce learned behavior and heritable mutation.

core_loop: play the current ruler -> manage vassal opinion, council, and stress -> arrange marriages, schemes, and wars over claims -> ruler dies -> heir inherits titles under succession law -> realm fragments or consolidates
design_notes: CK3 makes the player a character rather than a state: realm strength depends on vassals whose itemized opinions, traits, and family ties decide whether they serve or rebel. Succession laws make death the main source of disruption, and stress penalizes playing a character against type, which pushes players to roleplay their traits. Event content is authored but fired from on_actions and character state, so the same templates produce different stories in different courts; culture and religion conversion is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal culture-religion-conversion).

mechanics.note: On death, play passes to the player heir and titles pass under the realm's succession law, so partition can split a realm among children; the game ends if no viable heir remains, and dynasty heads spend Renown on bonuses for every dynasty member.
Personality, education, and genetic traits modify the six skills (Diplomacy, Martial, Stewardship, Intrigue, Learning, Prowess), opinions, and which event options a character can take.

Each character's opinion of another is an itemized list of modifiers from traits, relations, actions, and events, many expiring over time; discontented vassals join factions pressing for independence, a rival claimant, or less crown authority.
Skills grow from education and from perks in six lifestyles, each with three skill trees.
Friends, rivals, and lovers form between characters and shift opinions and event outcomes.
Marriages create alliances and heirs, making match choice a political decision.
Genetic traits such as strong or poor health pass to children.
Vassal factions accumulate strength and can revolt when their demands are refused.
Wars are fought over claims, and marriages and alliances link realms.
Events are called from on_actions, decisions, and interactions, with weighted options and scheduled follow-ups.
Lifestyle perk trees and cultural innovations unlock abilities and buildings.
Nested tooltips let players open explanations of terms inside other tooltips.

Acting against personality traits and suffering events add stress; crossing stress levels fires mental-break events whose coping options can add traits (from level 2 up), and extreme stress can kill the character.
Prestige and piety accrue from rank, traits, and deeds and are spent on actions such as creating titles (prestige) and faith decisions (piety).
Counties carry a faith and a culture; the court chaplain can convert a county's faith and the steward can promote the ruler's culture, while faith hostility sets opinion penalties from 0 to -30.
Counties belong to titles with de jure hierarchies, and wars are fought to press claims on them; conquered counties start with low county control.
War score from battles and occupation lets the attacker enforce the war goal at full score, while either side can offer white peace.
Battles resolve from army size, men-at-arms, knights, commander skill, and terrain, in phases that run until one side is routed.

name: Crusader Kings III
summary: A character-driven grand strategy game in which the player rules as successive heads of a medieval dynasty from 867 or later to 1453, managing traits, stress, vassal opinion, marriages, and succession across a map of feudal titles.

claims.text: The `year` value records 2008, when DCS: Black Shark, the first standalone DCS title, was released; the free DCS World platform entered open beta in May 2012.

core_loop: pick a module and mission -> cold start through cockpit switches -> fly and navigate -> find targets with sensors -> employ weapons and survive defenses -> recover and land -> debrief
design_notes: DCS treats each aircraft as a set of subsystems (engines, fuel, electrical, hydraulics, radios, sensors) operated through individually clickable cockpit controls, so procedures and failures follow from system state rather than scripts. Its fidelity reaches professional use: the U.S. Air Force's 355th Training Squadron has used the A-10C module, and French and Ukrainian pilots have trained on modules. The business model is a free base with two aircraft and two maps, with paid aircraft and map modules from Eagle Dynamics and third parties sharing one client.

mechanics.note: Aircraft modules are built from real-world data; the F-16C uses a professional flight model with a fly-by-wire flight control system.
Clickable cockpits operate modeled engines, fuel, electrical, hydraulic, and radio systems, so start-up and weapon employment follow real procedures.
Missions pit aircraft against air and ground units with sensors and weapons; users host PvE and PvP servers running their own missions.
The mission editor builds single-player and multiplayer missions with Lua scripting.
Lua mission scripting and third-party module development extend the platform.
Missiles, bombs, and gun rounds fly as simulated projectiles, so release parameters such as speed, altitude, and range decide hits.
Modules carry damage models, revised over the platform's development, so hits degrade the aircraft's modeled systems and how it flies.

name: DCS World
summary: A combat flight sim platform of study-level aircraft modules with clickable cockpits and modeled subsystems, flown in missions and on multiplayer servers built with a Lua-scriptable mission editor.

core_loop: spend political capital to adjust policy sliders -> effects propagate through the weighted policy network -> statistics, situations, and voter group happiness shift -> resolve dilemmas and events -> make election promises -> win or lose the election
design_notes: Democracy 4 models a country as one visible causal graph: policies, statistics, situations, and voter groups are nodes, and the interface shows the weighted links in and out of each. The player is constrained by political capital, earned through loyal ministers and spent on policy changes, and by voters who belong to several groups at once. Political capital as a regenerating action currency is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal political-capital).

mechanics.note: Policies in seven areas (tax, economy, welfare, foreign policy, transport, law and order, public services) are sliders; the engine treats voters, groups, policies, ministers, and events as neurons in a homebrew network with bounded values, so weighted effects move statistics such as crime and air quality and the happiness of voter groups.
Before each general election the player makes two promises to the electorate; broken promises raise voter cynicism, and losing the election ends the game.

Voter groups such as the religious, patriotic, parents, capitalists, socialists, liberals, and conservatives overlap, since each voter belongs to several, so pleasing every group is nearly impossible.
Dilemmas, such as appointing a senior judge, must be resolved before the turn can end.
Introducing or cancelling a policy costs political capital.
Excessive taxes cause tax evasion.
Deficits add to national debt that the player must pay down.
Situations such as pollution or homelessness persist while conditions hold, and events arrive outside player control.
Political capital, earned through loyal ministers, is spent each turn to introduce, cancel, or adjust policies, so it caps how fast the government can change.

name: Democracy 4
summary: A turn-based government sim in which the player, as leader of a democracy, adjusts policy sliders whose weighted effects move statistics and overlapping voter groups, resolves dilemmas, and tries to balance the budget and win the next election.

core_loop: explore a generated world by day -> gather and craft tools, food, and light -> manage hunger, health, and sanity -> survive nights, hounds, and seasons -> build a base and stockpile for winter -> die and start a new world
design_notes: Three meters interact: empty hunger drains health, and sanity falls at dusk and night and from unpleasant actions until, below 15% of maximum, shadow creatures attack, so the mind is a survival stock alongside the body. The 8-minute day is divided into day, dusk, and night segments whose split shifts with the season, and total darkness is lethal because Charlie attacks anyone without a light. Hound attacks escalate on a schedule tied to days survived, and death deletes the world except through rare resurrection items. Klei released it in beta in 2012 and fully on 23 April 2013.

mechanics.note: Hunger, health, and sanity meters; default maximum hunger is 150 and drains 75 per game day, and at empty hunger health drains 1.25 per second until the player eats or dies.
Recipes combine gathered items into tools, light, shelter, and weapons; most must first be prototyped at a crafting station such as the science machine, though some characters bypass this.

A day lasts 8 real minutes in sixteen 30-second segments of day, dusk, and night; sanity drains 5 per minute at dusk and 50 per minute in total darkness, where Charlie attacks unless the player has light.
Winter shortens days and lengthens nights; seasons change hazards.
Hound attacks scale with days survived, from 2 hounds every 5-8 days early to 7-10 hounds every 11-16 days after day 100, with shorter warnings.
Food spoils over time; spoiled food restores less hunger and costs health and sanity.
Picked grass, saplings, and berry bushes regrow.
Fire spreads across flammable plants and structures.
Each world is randomly generated.
Death deletes the world unless a rare resurrection item is available.

name: Don't Starve
summary: A survival sim in a procedurally generated wilderness where the player balances hunger, health, and sanity, crafts tools and light, and prepares for darkness, hounds, and seasons.

aliases: Slaves to Armok: God of Blood Chapter II: Dwarf Fortress
core_loop: embark and dig -> designate jobs, stockpiles, and workshops -> dwarves self-assign labors and craft -> needs, emotions, and stress accumulate -> migrants, caravans, sieges, and beasts arrive -> fortress thrives or collapses into the world's legends
design_notes: Tarn Adams's stated principles are to break a system into parts, avoid overplanning, and base each model on a real-world analog; he describes the game as a story generator. The fortress is embarked inside a world whose geology and history were already simulated, and the fortress's own events flow back into that history through Legends, so a collapse becomes a record that a later adventurer can visit. Strange moods let an inspired dwarf seize a workshop to make a named artifact and go insane if materials are missing, which turns the production system into a story source. The game was free and donation-funded from 2006; a paid Steam edition with sprite graphics followed in December 2022, still short of a 1.0 version.

mechanics.note: World generation builds elevation, rainfall, drainage, temperature, and vegetation layers, then simulates civilizations, sites, and historical figures for a player-chosen number of years before the fortress is embarked.
The player designates digging, chopping, construction, and workshop jobs; dwarves with the matching labor enabled pick them up, and a manager can queue work orders automatically.

Emotions add to or subtract from a hidden stress value (-1,000,000 to +1,000,000) with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000; stressed dwarves throw tantrums, fall into depression, or wander obliviously, prolonged stress leads to insanity, and one breakdown can spread unhappiness.

Body parts are layered tissues (skin, fat, muscle, bone, nerves) damaged individually in combat; injuries can be permanent and are treated in a hospital with traction benches, casts, sutures, and splints.
Water and magma flow tile by tile with up to seven depth levels per tile, so breaching a river, cavern lake, or magma source floods connected tunnels.
Z-levels, added in 2007, let the fortress descend level by level through soil and stone to caverns, the magma sea, and the underworld, connected by stairs and ramps.
Legends mode lists historical figures, sites, artifacts, and civilizations with a historical map; fortress deeds and retired adventurers are added, and the archive exports to XML.
Work quality and speed rise with skill gained through practice in each labor.
Food, drink, and sleep, plus personal needs such as socializing or praying met at taverns, temples, and libraries.
Emotions become short-term memories; strong or revisited ones are promoted to long-term memories that keep adding stress.
Facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale how stress builds and dissipates.
Friends, family, and pets; their deaths are major stressors.
Ore is smelted to bars and alloyed; steel needs flux to make pig iron plus coke or charcoal, and magma can replace fuel.
Tiles, materials, and creatures carry temperatures.
Fires spread and burn dwarves and furniture.
Ambushes, sieges, megabeasts, and forgotten beasts are met with squads, fortifications, and traps triggered by levers or pressure plates.
Wealthier and more populous fortresses attract sieges and megabeasts.
Migrant waves from the mountainhome grow as the fortress develops.
Yearly caravans from neighboring civilizations are handled by a broker; caravans can be absent or hostile depending on history.
Furniture defines bedrooms, dining halls, and offices; nobles demand rooms of rising value.
A justice system punishes assault, murder, and vandalism.
Underground farming on soil layers; plump helmet mushrooms are brewed into wine.
Dwarves carry goods to player-defined stockpiles.
Military squads in uniforms train at barracks and can be ordered to attack.

Emotions from events add to or subtract from a hidden stress value (-1,000,000 to +1,000,000) scaled by facets such as stress vulnerability and bravery; above +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000 dwarves risk tantrums, depression, obliviousness, and insanity, and long-term memories keep adding stress.

name: Dwarf Fortress
summary: A colony sim in which the player directs a fortress of autonomous dwarves inside a procedurally generated world whose history, geology, fluids, bodies, and minds are all simulated.

claims.text: Dyson Sphere Program was still labeled Early Access on Steam when accessed in October 2026, so no full-release year is recorded.
Reviewers compare it favorably to Factorio and Satisfactory, but the cited source names only Stellaris as a design inspiration, so no Factorio influence edge is recorded.

core_loop: mine planetary veins -> belt ores through smelters and assemblers -> craft matrix cubes for research -> link planets and stars with logistics stations -> launch solar sails and carrier rockets -> Dyson sphere power feeds endgame production
design_notes: Dyson Sphere Program scales the factory puzzle from one map to a randomly generated cluster of stars: each planet is a rotating sphere whose day-night cycle affects solar power, and logistics stations match per-item local and remote supply and demand, sending up to 100 drones within a planet and 10 vessels between planets or, with Space Warpers, between stars. The Dyson sphere is a megastructure designed in a node-and-frame editor and built by ejecting solar sails (36 kW each at base, scaled by star luminosity, expiring after 5,400 seconds unless captured by a completed shell) and launching carrier rockets; ray receivers return its energy to planets or convert it to critical photons. The December 2023 Dark Fog update added hives and planetary bases whose threat rises with the player's power generation and combat, a variant of pollution-driven aggression. The developers drew inspiration from Stellaris, which included Dyson sphere construction. The sphere works as a goal sink that absorbs very large quantities of sails and rockets; no taxonomy mechanic covers such megaproject sinks, so this run proposed one.

mechanics.note: Smelters, assemblers, chemical plants, refineries, and particle colliders run fixed recipes that build up to six matrix cube types and Dyson sphere components; proliferator coating adds extra products or speed.
Three belt tiers carry items between sorters and machines on a planetary grid that wraps around a sphere and narrows toward the poles.
Labs in research mode consume matrix cubes in technology-specific mixes, all stacked labs working on the front of one queue; labs can instead be switched to manufacture matrices.
Mining machines and advanced miners extract iron, copper, titanium, silicon, and rare veins whose distribution differs by planet and star type; pumps and oil extractors tap fluids.

Wind, thermal, solar, fusion, and artificial-star generators feed tower-linked grids; logistics stations charge at 30 to 300 MW, and Dyson sphere energy reaches planets through ray receivers at 30% base efficiency.
