Zone soil types and terrain affect outpost farming.
Research unlocks equipment and technologies.
Outposts must be defended against attackers.
Some weather, such as acid rain, harms characters.
Fights resolve from character combat skills, weapon stats, and armor, with damage applied to individual limbs.

name: Kenshi
summary: A squad-based open-world RPG with no hero character, where any recruit can starve, lose limbs, train skills by doing, be enslaved, or found an outpost among reactive factions.

core_loop: assemble a craft from parts -> launch and stage through the atmosphere -> plan maneuver nodes and burn for orbit or transfer -> land, dock, or crash -> return science, funds, and reputation -> unlock parts and design a more ambitious craft
design_notes: Stock orbits use a patched-conic approximation: a vessel is attracted by one body at a time and switches at sphere-of-influence boundaries, so there are no Lagrange points, but coasting vessels can be propagated on rails during time warp. Vessels are trees of parts joined by joints of limited strength, so mass distribution, thrust placement, and staging order decide whether a design flies, wobbles, or tears apart. Failure (stranded or dead Kerbals, debris) is a source of player stories rather than a hard stop, and Career mode layers funds, reputation, and contracts on top of the physics sandbox.

mechanics.note: Patched conics: a vessel orbits one body at a time and switches at sphere-of-influence boundaries; maneuver nodes preview delta-v and the resulting trajectory; planets ride fixed rails rather than n-body motion.

Craft are built in the Vehicle Assembly Building or Spaceplane Hangar from pods, tanks, engines, decouplers, wings, and science parts; part order sets the staging sequence, and each stage's mass, thrust, and fuel set its delta-v.
Each part is a rigid body joined to its parent with a joint of limited strength; excess force breaks joints, so tall stacks wobble and hard impacts shed parts or kill Kerbals.
Drag, lift, and control surfaces govern ascent profiles, spaceplanes, and aerobraking.
Atmospheric entry heats parts; heat shields absorb it and overheated parts are destroyed.
Science from experiments unlocks part nodes in Science and Career modes.
Career contracts pay for objectives such as reaching an orbit or testing a part, with deadlines and penalties.
Career funds pay for parts, fuel, crew, and facility upgrades; contract payouts are the income.
Career reputation rises with completed contracts and falls with failures and Kerbal deaths.
Manual ascents, landings, and docking reward piloting skill; SAS assists attitude hold.
Kerbals die in crashes and EVA accidents; Career mode costs reputation for deaths, and a difficulty option sets whether lost crews respawn.
Drills mine ore on planets and asteroids that converters turn into fuel, a system adopted from mods.
On-rails time warp skips long coasts; physics warp speeds powered flight at reduced stability.
C# plugins and part configs extend the game; mods such as Real Solar System and Principia replace the planetary system and the orbital model.
Parts are destroyed individually by impact or overheating, removing their engines, tanks, or controls from the craft.

name: Kerbal Space Program
summary: A space flight sim where the player assembles rockets from parts and flies them under patched-conic orbital physics and atmospheric aerodynamics through a scaled-down planetary system.

core_loop: place a keep and houses on an island -> peasants farm, cut wood, and quarry -> store food for the annual winter -> tax peasants to pay workers and unlock buildings -> stack castle blocks into walls and towers -> repel vikings, dragons, and ogres
design_notes: Kingdoms and Castles pairs a light town economy with a block-built castle: walls and towers form from how blocks are stacked, and taller archer towers reach farther, so defense is shaped geometry rather than a building menu. Each villager and resource is individually simulated, and an annual winter that destroys crops sets a regular survival check. Raiders kidnap peasants and burn buildings, and a dragon targets granaries, linking defense to food security.

mechanics.note: Vikings kidnap peasants, steal resources, and burn the town; dragons torch granaries; ogres attack; soldiers and archer towers defend.
An annual winter destroys crops, so food must be stored in granaries to prevent starvation.
Castle blocks stack into walls and towers whose shape forms automatically; taller archer towers have longer range.
Peasant taxes pay workers and unlock buildings.
Happiness from layout, churches, taverns, and festivals.
Happiness and housing attract new residents.
Lightning starts fires.
Plagues spread and must be healed.
Foresters cut and replant trees.
Diplomats make trade agreements, alliances, and wars with AI kingdoms.

name: Kingdoms and Castles
summary: A medieval town builder in which peasants farm and stockpile for an annual winter while the player stacks castle blocks into walls and towers to defend against vikings, dragons, and ogres.

core_loop: read the weather report -> choose glasses to make, signs to buy, and price per glass -> demand resolves into sales -> profit or a storm loss -> reinvest the next day
design_notes: Lemonade Stand reduces a business to three daily inputs (glasses made, advertising signs, price per glass) and one exogenous variable, the weather (sunny, cloudy, or hot and dry), which shifts demand. Shocks are random: thunderstorms on cloudy days wipe out the day's investment, and street closures or wind that blows signs away also occur. Up to 30 players can each run an independent stand under the same weather. Signs are an early case of advertising spend used as a demand lever; the taxonomy has no mechanic for marketing spend, so the run proposes advertising-awareness.

mechanics.note: Aggregate customers buy more at lower prices and with more advertising signs; sales are capped by the glasses made that day.
Each day is sunny, cloudy, or hot and dry, and the weather sets the demand level the price and sign choices act on.
Twelve rounds of one day each: the player makes decisions, the day resolves, and an earnings report follows.
Cash on hand limits how many glasses and signs can be bought each day.
Thunderstorms void a day's profits; street closures and blown-away signs also occur.
The weather for the day is shown before the player commits to production.
Advertising signs bought each day raise that day's demand alongside price and weather, with no carryover between days.

name: Lemonade Stand
summary: A 1973 educational business sim in which the player runs a lemonade stand for 12 days, setting glasses made, advertising signs, and price against a daily weather report.

core_loop: watch the resident's routine -> hunger, thirst, and mood drift -> deliver food, water, gifts, or pats -> type polite requests -> mood decides whether he complies -> repeat across sessions
design_notes: Rich Gold conceived the game and David Crane built it at Activision; the documentation presents the little people as real beings living inside the computer, with the player as their caretaker. Each disk's serial number seeded the resident's name (from 256), shirt color, personality, and behavior, so every copy hosted a different person. There is no win condition: the resident cooks, reads, plays piano, phones, and types letters about his feelings on a day of about six real-time hours, and his mood gates whether typed requests are obeyed. The cassette C64 version dropped memory, letters, and card games, which shows which systems carried the sense of a persistent person.

mechanics.note: Keyboard commands deliver food (CTRL+F), add water to his tank (CTRL+W), deliver dog food, pat him, or give records and books; a resident left unfed turns green and sick until he eats.
Hunger and thirst build between deliveries; unmet needs lower his mood and eventually make him visibly sick.
The disk serial number seeds his name from a pool of 256, his shirt color, personality, and behavior parameters.
He runs a routine of cooking, watching television, reading the newspaper, playing records, and dancing on a compressed day of about six real-time hours.
Typed requests such as 'Please play piano' are matched against a keyword vocabulary; politeness helps, and a sad or sick resident may refuse.
Seeded personality and mood parameters change which activities he prefers, how often he invites the player to cards or writes letters, and how readily he obeys.

name: Little Computer People
summary: A 1985 home-computer life sim in which one procedurally seeded little person lives in a cross-section of a three-story house, follows a daily routine, and depends on the player for food, water, and attention.

core_loop: draw curved roads and burgage plots -> families move in and staff workplaces -> fields, backyard extensions, and production chains feed the market -> taxes, tithes, and trade fund a retinue -> defend against bandits and rival lords
design_notes: Manor Lords drops the zoning grid: the player draws plots against freely curved roads, the game divides them into burgage plots, and households extend them with backyard gardens, chickens, or goats, so housing is also production. Fields carry soil fertility per crop that rotation preserves, and hunting depends on animal populations that overexpansion drives away. Militia levies come from the town's own families, so each battle death is a lost worker; the game remained in early access as of August 2026.

mechanics.note: Residential plots drawn along roads are divided into burgage plots that families build on and extend with backyard production.
Fields depend on soil fertility per crop; rotation and fallow maintain yields, and overuse exhausts soil.
Roads curve freely and plots and buildings take their shape from them.
Spring rains and winter snow change work and needs.
Raw materials pass through workshops into goods, weapons, and armor.
Households need basic goods and luxuries; shortfalls lower satisfaction.
Approval responds to supply, taxes, and tithes.
Six tax types, a yearly King's tax, and tithes on villagers.
Hunting grounds depend on animal populations; overexpansion drives deer away and deforests land.
Real-time battles with fatigue, weather, and equipment; retinue, mercenaries, and militia drawn from townspeople.
Bandit raids threaten the town and loot stores.
Surpluses sold to traveling merchants; imports and exports balanced through trade.

name: Manor Lords
summary: An early-access medieval city builder in which families settle gridless burgage plots along curved roads, fields depend on soil fertility and crop rotation, and the lord fields retinue and militia in real-time battles.

core_loop: pick aircraft, airport, and time -> preflight and start up -> take off into live or set weather -> navigate and hand-fly or use autopilot -> approach and land -> pick the next flight
design_notes: The world is data rather than authored terrain: Bing Maps imagery refreshed every 28 days, Blackshark.ai photogrammetry, and Azure AI 3D generation streamed from more than two petabytes, with Meteoblue weather and real air traffic fed in live. The flight model simulates over 1,000 control surfaces and wind over terrain, and a legacy model is kept as an option. No mechanic in the taxonomy covers simulation state driven by real-world data feeds (proposed as real-world-data-feeds).

mechanics.note: The physics engine computes forces over more than 1,000 control surfaces and models wind flowing over terrain; a legacy flight model option remains.
Meteoblue live global weather sets clouds, wind, and precipitation in real time, and wind interacts with the terrain model.
An in-game marketplace and third-party aircraft and airports extend the sim.

The whole Earth is built from Bing Maps imagery updated every 28 days and AI-generated 3D content streamed from more than two petabytes in the cloud, while Meteoblue live weather and live air traffic feed the sim at runtime.

name: Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020)
summary: A flight sim that streams a photorealistic model of the whole Earth built from map and photogrammetry data and flies aircraft through live weather with a surface-level aerodynamic model.

core_loop: choose a career job -> walk around the aircraft for preflight -> start systems -> fly the mission profile (firefighting, rescue, cargo hook, airline) -> earn experience, reputation, and certifications -> unlock specializations
design_notes: Career mode turns the 2020 sandbox into a progression game: aerial firefighting, search and rescue, crop dusting, helicopter cargo hook, outsize cargo in the Airbus Beluga, arctic cargo in the A400M, and airline flights are gated by certifications and specializations earned through experience and reputation. Aircraft physics and systems (electrical, fuel, pneumatic, hydraulic) were revised, and stones, gravel, and grass are modeled in 3D and affect wheels. The launch showed the cost of a streamed world: an overwhelmed database cache caused long loads and missing content.

mechanics.note: Aircraft physics were revised, and ground contact models 3D stones, gravel, and grass that affect wheels during takeoff, landing, and taxi.
Career jobs include aerial firefighting, search and rescue, crop dusting, helicopter cargo hook, Beluga outsize cargo, A400M arctic cargo, and airline passenger flights.
Starting from an airport the player chooses, experience earns certifications and specializations that unlock job types.
Career reputation accumulates alongside experience.
A walk-around preflight handles covers, doors, and service items, and revised electrical, fuel, pneumatic, and hydraulic systems gate start-up.
The pilot walks around the aircraft on foot during preflight.
The streamed whole-Earth world of the 2020 game continues, and the launch showed the dependence when an overwhelmed database cache caused long loads and missing content.

name: Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024
summary: The successor to Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) that adds a career mode of certified aviation jobs, walk-around preflight, revised aircraft systems, and modeled ground surfaces to the streamed whole-Earth flight sim.

claims.text: Mindustry was created for the April 2017 itch.io Metal Monstrosity game jam and came to Steam in 2019 (version 3, store date 2019-09-26).
Coverage compares Mindustry to Factorio, and its README describes it as an automation tower defense RTS; the influenced_by edge reflects that widely noted lineage rather than a developer statement.

core_loop: drill ore -> belt items to the core and factories -> build and supply turrets -> survive scheduled enemy waves -> research new blocks with core resources -> capture sectors and launch resources between them
design_notes: Mindustry began as a 2017 itch.io jam game and fuses Factorio-style belt logistics with tower defense: turrets consume belted ammunition, power, and coolant, so the factory's layout is the defense, and survival maps send progressively stronger waves at the core on a timer. Version 6 (2020) added RTS units built in factories and upgraded through reconstructors, and Mindustry Logic, an assembly-like language that runs on processor blocks, reads sensors and memory cells, and can bind and command units. The campaign spans Serpulo and Erekir with 35 hand-made maps and 250+ procedural sectors whose production continues while the player is elsewhere and is moved between sectors by launch pads. The game is GPL-3.0 and free from the author while also sold on Steam, so community servers, plugins, and mods are unrestricted.

mechanics.note: Conveyors, junctions, routers, sorters, overflow gates, and bridges move items from drills to the core, factories, and turret ammo inputs.
Smelters, presses, kilns, separators, and mixers turn copper, lead, sand, coal, titanium, and thorium into graphite, silicon, plastanium, and surge alloy.
Enemy waves spawn on a schedule and path toward the core; about 18 Serpulo and 10 Erekir turret types consume ammo items, liquids, or power, backed by walls, menders, and shield projectors.
Survival maps send progressively stronger waves with tougher unit types and bosses as wave numbers rise; the cited sources do not tie wave strength to the player's own wealth.
Mechanical, pneumatic, laser, and airblast drills mine ore tiles at speeds set by drill tier and ore hardness, with optional water boosting.

Micro, logic, and hyper processors run Mindustry Logic, an assembly-like language with one operation per instruction that reads sensors and memory cells, controls linked buildings and turrets, and binds units with ubind to command them.
A visible timer counts down to the next wave, and wave timing can be changed in custom game rules.
Over 250 technology blocks are researched by spending core resources along a tree that also gates campaign sectors.
Combustion, steam, solar, thorium, and impact generators feed node-linked grids with batteries; turrets, shields, and factories draw power.
Conduits carry water, slag, oil, and cryofluid; optional coolant and lubricant raise turret and factory rates.
Since version 7 units can be selected and commanded RTS-style, while others follow default AI or logic control.
Schematics save layouts as shareable text and are traded on Steam Workshop.
Campaign sectors set win conditions such as surviving a number of waves or destroying enemy cores on attack maps.
The GPL-3.0 source allows unrestricted mods, and community servers run plugins for custom maps and game modes.
Optional coolant and lubricant fed to turrets and factories raise their rates, and water boosts drill speed.

name: Mindustry
summary: An open-source automation tower defense game in which the player belts ore into factories that supply turrets, units, and the core against enemy waves while capturing campaign sectors on two planets, with an assembly-like logic language for controlling blocks and units.

core_loop: explore a generated world -> mine blocks and gather resources -> craft tools, armor, and workstations -> build shelter before night mobs spawn -> farm, breed, and trade -> dig deeper or travel to the Nether and End for rarer materials
design_notes: The world is an effectively infinite grid of one-meter blocks generated from a seed with biomes, caves, and ore distributions, and every block can be removed or placed, so terrain is both resource and building material. Survival pressure is light (hunger, health, light-level mob spawning on a 20-minute day cycle) and leaves room for self-set goals. Redstone gives the block world wires, power sources, repeaters, and pistons, which players use to build farms, logic gates, and working computers. The game began as a public alpha in May 2009 and reached 1.0 in November 2011.

mechanics.note: Worlds generate from a seed into biomes, caves, ravines, villages, and ore layers that vary by depth; terrain extends effectively without limit in horizontal directions.
A 2x2 inventory grid and a 3x3 crafting table turn blocks and items into tools, armor, and blocks from shaped recipes; furnaces, anvils, and enchanting tables extend the recipe set.
Blocks are mined by hand or with tools whose tier (wood, stone, iron, diamond, netherite) sets mining speed and which ores drop items.
Survival mode has health and hunger bars; food restores hunger, high hunger regenerates health, and starvation, falls, drowning, and mobs deal damage.
A 20-minute real-time day; hostile mobs spawn in low light, so night and caves are dangerous, and beds skip the night.
Any block can be placed on the voxel grid, so building has no fixed footprint.
Redstone dust carries power from levers, buttons, and sensors through repeaters and comparators to pistons, doors, and dispensers.
Crops grow in stages on farmland, faster with water nearby and light.
Passive mobs breed when fed their preferred food and yield food, wool, and leather.
Water and lava flow a limited number of blocks out from source blocks; where they meet they form cobblestone, stone, or obsidian.
Fire spreads to nearby flammable blocks such as wood and wool and burns them away.
Material tiers gate progression: iron tools mine diamonds, diamond tools mine obsidian, and Nether materials gate brewing and the End.
Java Edition mods (Forge, Fabric) and Bedrock add-ons, datapacks, and server plugins are widely used.
Public multiplayer servers and Realms host worlds that persist for many players.
On death in survival the player's inventory and some experience drop at the death site and despawn after a few minutes if not recovered.

name: Minecraft
summary: A procedurally generated voxel sandbox where players mine blocks, craft tools, survive hostile night mobs and hunger, farm and trade, and build circuits from redstone.

core_loop: new stations appear -> draw or reroute lines -> trains carry shape-matched passengers -> weekly grant of new assets -> demand outgrows capacity -> a station overcrowds and the run ends
design_notes: Mini Metro abstracts a metro network into station shapes, passengers drawn as the shape of the station type they want to reach, and a scarce inventory of lines, locomotives, tunnels, and bridges. New stations keep appearing while supply arrives only as a weekly grant, so the player keeps redrawing a network that is always under capacity. Failure is local and visible: a station over its limit (typically six passengers) for long enough ends the run. Modes vary the rules: Extreme fixes lines once placed, Endless removes overcrowding, and Creative is a sandbox.

mechanics.note: The player draws colored lines between stations and assigns trains that load and unload automatically; ridership is the score.
Passengers wait at stations with limited capacity, typically six; interchanges raise capacity and loading speed, and a station overcrowded too long ends the game.
Passengers ride to any station of their target shape, transferring between lines when needed.
Each in-game week grants extra rolling stock and a choice of assets such as tunnels, bridges, new lines, or interchanges.
Time can be paused to reroute lines or move trains.

name: Mini Metro
summary: A minimalist subway-design game where the player draws and redraws lines between shape-coded stations under a weekly ration of trains and tunnels until a station overcrowds.

core_loop: design and build car parts -> hire drivers, designers, and mechanics -> set race weekend strategy -> race simulates with tyre, fuel, and weather calls -> results earn money and standing -> develop next season's car
design_notes: Motorsport Manager splits the job into a between-races engineering game and a live race game. Between races the player commissions car parts and chooses which go into next season's car, trading performance against development time. During races the simulation runs in real time with pause, and the player decides tyre compounds, pit timing, and whether to gamble on a fast pit stop or stay on slicks as dynamic weather changes. Drivers have personality types that cause team drama and respond to tough love or support. A simpler mobile game of the same name was released on iOS in 2014; this entry covers the 2016 PC game.

mechanics.note: Races are simulated in real time from driver attributes, car part performance, tyres, fuel, and weather, with the player intervening on strategy.
Car parts are designed and built over time, rated on performance, and chosen for next season's car, which sets pace at pre-season testing.
Drivers, team managers, mechanics, and designers are hired; skilled mechanics shorten pit stops.
Dynamic weather during sessions forces calls such as switching to intermediates or staying on slicks.
Drivers have distinct personality types that cause team drama and respond differently to tough love or support.
Tyres wear over a stint and car parts lose condition, so strategy balances pace against wear.
Prize money and sponsor income fund salaries and part development.
Races run in real time with pause and speed controls.
Driver and staff contracts are negotiated over wages, length, and bonuses, and candidates can reject offers and end talks.
The chairman sets objectives each season, and missing them lowers the chairman's confidence until the player is fired.

name: Motorsport Manager
summary: A racing team management game in which the player designs car parts across seasons, hires drivers and staff, and makes live strategy calls on tyres, pit stops, and weather while races are simulated.

core_loop: claim a land grant -> buy and outfit M.U.L.E.s and walk them to plots -> production with shortages and random events -> real-time auctions set prices -> buy or sell -> next round
design_notes: M.U.L.E. couples its four resources: food sets how long a player's development turn lasts, energy shortages stop plots from producing, and smithore supply sets M.U.L.E. prices and whether the store can manufacture more. Prices are set in real-time auctions in which buyers and sellers move avatars toward a price, so withholding goods and private deals between players are legitimate tactics. Danielle Bunten built catch-up rules into the systems: tied bids go to the player in the losing position, favorable events rarely hit the leader and harmful ones never hit last place, and land auctions were replaced by free grants because they compounded the leader's advantage. The taxonomy has no mechanic for systematic catch-up rules (proposed as catch-up-balancing).

mechanics.note: Each round resources trade in a real-time auction: sellers and buyers walk avatars toward a price line, trades fire when they meet, and ties go to the trailing player.
Store prices respond to supply: refusing to sell raises a resource's price in later rounds, and smithore scarcity raises the price of new M.U.L.E.s.
A M.U.L.E. outfitted for food, energy, smithore, or crystite harvests its plot each round; output depends on terrain and the plot's development.
Rounds run in fixed phases: land grant, timed development, production, then auctions for each resource.
Plots grouped with others producing the same resource get a production bonus.
Each player needs food and energy each round; low food shortens the next development turn and low energy stops some plots.
The store turns smithore into new M.U.L.E.s; with no smithore it cannot build more.
Sunspots, pirate raids, meteorites, and runaway M.U.L.E.s, targeted away from the last-place player.
Computer opponents fill empty seats and compete for plots and auction trades.
Players walk a colonist through town to buy and outfit M.U.L.E.s and lead them to plots under a turn timer.

name: M.U.L.E.
summary: A four-player economic strategy game on a colony planet where players outfit M.U.L.E. robots to produce food, energy, smithore, and crystite and trade them in real-time auctions.

core_loop: care for the dog by touch -> teach tricks by voice -> walk the dog and find items -> enter disc, agility, and obedience trials -> earn prize money and trainer points -> buy supplies and unlock new breeds
design_notes: Nintendogs was built to show off DS hardware: the touchscreen handles petting, grooming, and washing, and the microphone handles the dog's name and trick commands. Care runs on the DS clock, so hunger, thirst, and coat condition worsen with elapsed time, but dogs cannot die, breed, or age, which makes neglect a recoverable setback rather than a fail state. Trials have five classes from Beginner to Championship, and placing third or better promotes a dog. Bark Mode lets nearby players' dogs meet and exchange presents.

mechanics.note: Touch petting, brushing, and washing plus food and water bowls maintain hunger, thirst, and coat condition; walks, balls, discs, and toys add play.
When the dog strikes a pose such as sit, the player records a spoken command; repeating the pairing teaches the trick, and the dog later responds to the voice cue.
The microphone recognizes the dog's name and trick words by matching the player's voice against recorded samples.
Hunger, thirst, and dirtiness worsen with real elapsed time.
Care state advances with the DS internal clock and calendar.
Trial prize money and trainer points unlock new breeds and supplies.
Bark Mode lets nearby DS owners meet each other's dogs and exchange presents.

name: Nintendogs
summary: A Nintendo DS puppy sim in which the player pets, washes, feeds, and walks up to three dogs, teaches them tricks with recorded voice commands, and enters disc, agility, and obedience trials.

core_loop: descend into a procedurally generated biome -> fight enemies with wands that also reshape the pixel world -> survive fire, liquids, and gases set off by fighting -> buy or find spells and rebuild wands at the Holy Mountain -> descend again or die and restart
design_notes: Noita's Falling Everything engine simulates each pixel as a material with state (solid, powder, liquid, gas) and reaction rules, and solid bodies are Box2D rigid bodies that break into pixels when damaged. Because spells, enemies, and the player all act on that layer, combat routinely sets off chain events such as burning oil, steam explosions, flooding, and collapsing ceilings, and these kill the player as often as enemies do. Wand building composes spells with modifiers into programs with cast order and mana limits, and runs are permadeath.

mechanics.note: Every pixel of terrain is a material that falls, flows, or rises by local rules, so digging, explosions, and spills reshape the level in real time.
Materials react by rule: lava and water form rock and steam, wood burns into smoke, acid eats terrain, and alchemical liquids such as polymorphine or teleportatium apply their effects on contact.
A death ends the run and the world is regenerated; only some unlocks, such as new spells in the pool, persist.
Wands have stats such as capacity, mana, recharge, and cast delay; spells and modifiers placed in a wand's slots execute in order, so arrangement changes what the wand does.
Box2D rigid bodies such as crates, bricks, and detached terrain chunks can be kicked, thrown, and shattered.
Fire spreads through wood, grass, oil, and gunpowder and burns the player and enemies alike.
Liquids pool and flow and gases rise and spread through caves at pixel level.
Each seed generates biome layouts from hand-made tile pieces within a fixed order of biomes.
The player controls one witch with levitation, kicking, and wand casting.
Lua-based mods are supported and distributed through Steam Workshop.
Each world seed defines two secret alchemy recipes (Lively Concoction and Alchemic Precursor), each made from three materials that players must find by experiment.

name: Noita
summary: A roguelite action game in which every pixel of the world is simulated as a falling-sand material that burns, melts, flows, and reacts, and the player builds wands from spells to dig through procedurally generated levels.

core_loop: land an HQ -> claim tiles and build extractors -> refine resources into goods -> sell into a market whose prices move with each trade -> buy black market sabotage and stock -> buy out every rival
design_notes: Soren Johnson replaced combat with a shared market: 13 resources trade at prices that move with every purchase and sale, so selling a large stockpile drives the price down and one player's bulk purchases create openings for others. Black market items such as nukes, EMPs, and mutinies act through the economy, and each purchase raises the price of the next one. Victory comes from equity: players buy shares in rivals until they hold a majority of every company, and buying back one's own shares makes a takeover more expensive. Johnson names M.U.L.E. and Railroad Tycoon as inspirations.

mechanics.note: Each of 13 resources has a market price that falls when players sell and rises when they buy, with shortages and gluts driving rapid swings.
Players buy shares in rival companies and win by holding a majority of every company; debt lowers stock price, and buying back one's own stock raises buyout cost.
Extractors on claimed hex tiles mine water, aluminum, iron, silicon, and carbon at rates set by tile richness.
Steel mills, glass kilns, electronics factories, greenhouses, and hydrolysis reactors turn raw resources into higher-value goods and life support.
Up to eight companies, AI or human, compete in one market and attack each other through black market sabotage such as nukes, EMPs, and mutinies.
Some resource tiles and patents are sold by auction.
Each HQ consumes life support resources such as water, food, oxygen, and power, which must be produced or bought.
Companies can run into debt, which depresses their share price.
Patents and HQ upgrades unlock buildings and bonuses.
Each match generates a new Martian map, so resource layouts and claims differ.

name: Offworld Trading Company
summary: A real-time economic strategy game on Mars where companies claim resource tiles, refine goods for a shared market whose prices move with every trade, and win by buying out every rival's stock.

claims.text: Opus Magnum is a refined version of Zach Barth's 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering, which is not in this dataset; the influenced_by edge to SpaceChem records Barth's shared instruction-grid and histogram design rather than a stated influence in the cited encyclopedia.
A Nintendo Switch version, Opus Magnum The Complete Edition, released on 2026-03-17.

core_loop: read the reagents and product -> place arms, tracks, and glyphs on the hex grid -> write instructions on the timeline -> run until the required products are made -> compare cost, cycles, and area histograms -> export a looping GIF or optimize
design_notes: Opus Magnum refines Zach Barth's 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering into Zachtronics' most permissive puzzle design: there is no part limit, any machine that delivers the products counts, and the difficulty is choosing among three competing metrics. Arms grab, rotate, pivot, extend, and move on tracks under a per-arm instruction tape, and glyphs bond, unbond, calcify, and project metals one step toward gold. Solutions are ranked on cost in gold, cycles, and area, with no in-game reward for optimizing, so motivation comes from friends' scores and the histograms. Barth's experience with solution recording in Infinifactory led to built-in export of seamlessly looping GIFs, which made solutions shareable outside the game; a puzzle editor feeds Steam Workshop.

mechanics.note: Each arm has a row on a shared instruction timeline of grab, drop, rotate, pivot, extend, retract, and track moves; the machine loops the program until the required number of products is output.
Solutions are scored on cost in gold, cycles to complete, and area in hex tiles, with the community adding an unofficial sum metric.
Cost, cycles, and area are shown on histograms of all players' scores and against friends' scores; Zachtronics deliberately attaches no rewards to optimization.

A machine is assembled from arms, extendable arms, tracks, and glyphs of bonding, unbonding, calcification, and projection, plus devices such as Van Berlo's wheel, with no limit on parts beyond their cost.
Each puzzle fixes the input reagents and the required product molecule; chapters must be completed to advance.
A puzzle editor publishes solvable user puzzles to Steam Workshop, curated puzzles appear in the Journal of Alchemical Engineering, and solutions export as looping GIFs.

name: Opus Magnum
summary: A programming puzzle game in which the player builds alchemical machines from arms, tracks, and glyphs on a hex grid, programs them on an instruction timeline, and compares each looping solution's cost, cycles, and area against other players' histograms.

core_loop: buy supplies at the outset and at forts -> choose food consumption and pace each leg -> random events, weather, and illness hit the party -> hunt for food and cross rivers -> reach Oregon or die on the trail
design_notes: Three student teachers wrote it in two weeks for a Minneapolis classroom, where it debuted on 3 December 1971; MECC distributed it on its time-sharing network from 1975 and on the Apple II from 1980. The 1971 model is a few stocks (food, bullets, clothing, supplies, cash) spent over about twelve two-week rounds, with one or two random events and weather drawn each round and typed hunting that rewards speed. The 1985 graphical version added adjustable pace and rations, river crossings by fording, caulking, or ferry, a party of five, professions that set difficulty and score, and tombstones left by earlier players.
developer: Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann, and Paul Dillenberger; later MECC

mechanics.note: Food, clothing, and medical supplies are stocks drawn down each round at a player-chosen consumption rate; low food, cold without clothing, and untreated illness kill the traveler.
Each round closes with one or two random events and weather, such as storms, wagon breakdowns, snakebites, or attacks, that cost supplies or health.
The trip is a sequence of two-week rounds with fixed phases: stop at a fort or not, hunt or not, set consumption, then travel and resolve events.
Weather each round affects travel and illness.
Dead party members are gone; the 1985 version leaves a tombstone with an epitaph.

name: The Oregon Trail
summary: An educational turn-based travel sim in which the player buys supplies and sets rations for a wagon journey to Oregon while random events, weather, and illness threaten the party.

core_loop: scout and draft players -> set rosters, lineups, and depth charts -> simulate games pitch by pitch -> players develop or decline -> trade, sign, and manage finances -> build a franchise across seasons
design_notes: OOTP simulates baseball pitch by pitch from player ratings and reports it as scrolling play-by-play text with a minimal diamond, plus 3D ballparks and ball flight from OOTP 15. Its range of setups defines it: real current leagues under the MLB and Minor League Baseball licenses from OOTP 16, historical play that drops the player into any era with real rookies arriving each season, and fictional leagues. Ratings are filtered through scouting, so the GM sees estimates rather than true values. The league keeps a full statistical history with HTML reports, so long careers build an almanac.

mechanics.note: Games are simulated pitch by pitch from batter, pitcher, and fielder ratings and managerial settings, in real time, pitch-by-pitch control, or bulk simulation.
Player ratings are shown through a scout's evaluation, so accuracy depends on the scouting staff; the system was recoded in OOTP 14.
The GM signs free agents, drafts amateurs, and hires managers, coaches, and scouts within a budget.
Player ratings develop and decline over careers, including fielding development added in OOTP 14.
Players age, retire, and are replaced by drafts and historical debuts.
Fictional players are generated for fictional leagues and amateur drafts.
League histories, records, and player careers are stored and exported as HTML reports.
Franchise finances cover payroll, revenue, and budgets; the system was reworked in OOTP 16.
Extensive statistics and reports cover every player, team, and season.

Contract offers to free agents and extensions to rostered players are accepted or rejected against each player's demands, and trades are proposed to AI general managers who accept, reject, or counter.
Owners set expectations, and the general manager's job security falls when results and finances miss them, ending in dismissal.

name: Out of the Park Baseball
summary: A text-based baseball management sim in which the player runs a franchise's roster, scouting, draft, trades, and finances while a pitch-by-pitch engine simulates games for career, historical, or fictional leagues.

core_loop: dig into the asteroid -> lay out rooms, pipes, and wires -> duplicants perform prioritized errands -> oxygen, heat, germs, and waste redistribute tile by tile -> stress and shortfalls surface -> rebuild toward closed, sustainable loops
design_notes: Each cell holds one element with a mass and a temperature, and heat moves between cells every 0.2 s tick by conduction, so insulation, phase changes, and overheating machines follow from one rule rather than from per-building scripts. Most machines emit byproducts (a natural gas generator makes 800 W plus polluted water and carbon dioxide), so the long game is closing loops so waste becomes input. Mood uses a morale-versus-expectation gap: learning skills raises a duplicant's expectation, so better-trained colonists need better food, rooms, and decor. Wikipedia names Dwarf Fortress, Prison Architect, and The Sims as design influences.

mechanics.note: Every tile holds one gas, liquid, or solid with a mass; gases diffuse and equalize when a chamber is opened, and liquids drain under gravity, so breathable oxygen must be produced and carbon dioxide managed.

Cells exchange heat each 0.2 s tick with q = dT x dt x k x 1000, with multipliers for solid-gas and liquid-liquid contact; insulated tiles divide conductivity, and temperature thresholds melt, freeze, boil, or damage things.
Machines and duplicants emit polluted water, polluted oxygen, carbon dioxide, and heat; a natural gas generator consumes 90 g/s of gas for 800 W and outputs 67.5 g/s polluted water and 22.5 g/s CO2.
Gas and liquid pipes carry packets between buildings; a liquid pipe segment holds 10 kg and moves packets once per second, capping a line at 10 kg/s, and pipe contents exchange heat with their tiles.

Morale is the sum of timed buffs (Mess Hall +3, Private Bedroom +3, food up to +16, decor up to +12) compared to an expectation that rises with skills learned; each point under adds 2.5% stress per cycle up to 25%, full stress triggers a stress response, and 8 or more points over can trigger overjoyed responses.
Every errand carries a priority, and each duplicant has per-errand-type priorities on the Priorities screen; duplicants pick the highest available errand and favor tasks they are good at.
Dig, build, mop, and deconstruct orders placed on tiles.
Germs live on tiles, items, gases, and liquids; exposure past per-germ thresholds gives a contraction chance of 0.5 - 0.5 x tanh(resistance / 4).
Coal, hydrogen, natural gas, and manual generators on wires and batteries; overloaded circuits take damage.
Automation wires, sensors, and logic gates control doors, pumps, and generators; extended by the Automation Innovation update.
Skill points are spent on skills, which raise morale expectations.
Traits such as Germ Resistant or Allergies change resistances and stress reactions.
Enclosed rooms that meet requirements become Mess Halls, Bedrooms, and similar rooms that grant morale buffs.
Decor around a duplicant is compared to its recent average and feeds morale.
Plants need specific temperatures, atmospheres, and irrigation.
Critters are ranched for food and for their conversion of inputs into useful outputs.
Food rots unless refrigerated or kept in a sterile atmosphere.
Oxygen, temperature, power, plumbing, and germ overlays show hidden cell state.
Research unlocks buildings.
Asteroids are procedurally generated.

name: Oxygen Not Included
summary: A side-view colony sim in which a few duplicants survive inside an asteroid where every tile holds an element with mass and temperature, so air, liquids, heat, and germs flow through the base.

core_loop: read the day's rules -> inspect each entrant's papers -> interrogate, fingerprint, or scan discrepancies -> stamp approve, deny, or detain -> citations and bribes adjust pay -> pay rent, food, and heat -> next day adds rules
design_notes: The inspection rules are predicates that accumulate day by day as the fictional state's politics shift, so the same entrant generator yields harder cases over time. Pay is per correctly processed entrant within a fixed shift and citations arrive by fax after each error, which makes speed and accuracy a direct trade. The household ledger converts that trade into moral pressure, and bribes and rule-bending choices feed scripted branches that lead to twenty endings.

mechanics.note: Each day adds or changes entry requirements; the player cross-checks passports, permits, and other papers, can interrogate, compare fingerprints, or order body scans, and receives faxed citations after protocol violations.
Each shift is a fixed real-time working day and pay is per properly processed entrant, so processing speed trades against error risk.
The end-of-day ledger adds wages and bribes, subtracts citation penalties, and requires paying rent, food, heat, and other necessities; going into debt ends the game.
Family members' condition worsens on days when food, heat, or other necessities go unpaid.
Scripted entrants pose choices such as admitting a supposed spouse without complete papers, trading rule compliance against helping people.
EZIC contacts and other scripted encounters branch the story toward twenty endings, including escape to Obristan.
Randomly generated entrants are mixed with scripted ones; the unlockable endless mode uses only generated entrants.

name: Papers, Please
summary: A border inspection game in which the player checks entrants' documents against daily-changing rules on a timed shift and spends the wages on a family's rent, food, and heat.

core_loop: design Parafolks in the Paramaker -> build a grid-less home -> Parafolks pursue needs and wants -> socialize, work, and build skills around town -> relationships, children, and aging change the household -> share homes and Parafolks on the Workshop
design_notes: Paralives began as Alex Massé's solo project, was funded through Patreon (over 15,000 supporters by November 2023), and entered Steam early access on 2026-05-25 with about two years planned before 1.0. Its building tools are its most distinctive system: walls and furniture resize, recolor, and stack, walls can curve, floors can split level, and a road-style wall tool was inspired by Cities: Skylines. Conversation fills a together bar that unlocks together cards, multiselect lets several Parafolks act as a group, and procedural animation adapts to preceding animations.

mechanics.note: Grid-less building with curved walls, split-level floors, and resizable, recolorable, stackable furniture; walls are drawn with a road-style tool modeled on Cities: Skylines.
Parafolks carry needs, wants, and emotions that steer their autonomous behavior and set the player's care tasks.
Conversation fills a together bar between two Parafolks, and a full bar unlocks together cards.
Jobs with flexible career progression paths.
Steam Workshop distributes community houses, Parafolks, and mods.
An in-game modding interface lets players edit or add content.

name: Paralives
summary: An indie life sim, in early access since May 2026, in which players build grid-less homes and guide Parafolks with needs, emotions, traits, skills, and careers in an open-world town.

core_loop: accept an email job -> order parts with a shipping tier -> open the case and diagnose or assemble -> install software, remove viruses, or overclock -> benchmark -> get paid -> pay rent and electricity -> unlock better parts
design_notes: Parts are licensed real components with compatibility rules, and a machine's performance is measured with the real 3DMark benchmark, so a build's quality is an output of its parts rather than a designer-set score. Assembly has physical consequences: a CPU cooler mounted without thermal paste lets the processor overheat and fail. The career wraps this in a small business with monthly rent and electricity, accept-or-reject email jobs, and timed jobs that become more common later.
developer: Claudiu Kiss and The Irregular Corporation

mechanics.note: Email jobs ask for virus removal, upgrades, fixes, or overclocking on customer PCs; the player opens the case, identifies the faulty or missing part, and swaps it.
PCs are assembled from licensed cases, motherboards, CPUs, coolers, GPUs, memory, and storage; part choice and installation details such as thermal paste decide whether and how well the machine runs.
Customer requests, discount alerts, spam, and scams arrive in an inbox; accepted orders left unfulfilled are rejected, and timed jobs grow more common as the career advances.
3DMark benchmarking scores built or repaired machines.
Leveling up from job experience unlocks more advanced parts.
Monthly rent and electricity bills must be paid or the player incurs debt.

name: PC Building Simulator
summary: A workshop sim in which the player takes email jobs to build, upgrade, repair, and overclock PCs from licensed parts and verifies the results with benchmark software.

core_loop: lay out housing, roads, and floodplain farms -> the yearly Nile flood waters the farms -> walkers deliver services, food, and goods to houses -> houses evolve and pay taxes -> appease five gods and build monuments to meet mission goals
design_notes: Pharaoh reuses Caesar III's walker model and adds a calendar driven by the Nile: floodplain farms can only be worked between floods, irrigation ditches raise fertility, and the god Osiris can improve or worsen the flood. Monuments need worker facilities and delivered materials and take in-game years, a construction-logistics system with no exact taxonomy match (see run proposal). Five gods (Ra, Bast, Osiris, Ptah, Seth) grant gifts when appeased with shrines and temples and send disasters when angered.

mechanics.note: Fire marshals, constables, and other service walkers roam roads from their buildings and cover the houses they pass.
Housing improves in level when demands for goods, services, and surroundings are met.
A yearly Nile flood waters floodplain farms; irrigation ditches extend fertile land, and Osiris can raise or lower the flood quality.
Floodplain and meadow farms yield by fertility and season.
The flood season fixes when floodplain land can be farmed.
Houses need food and goods to advance.
Raw materials and goods trade with other cities for money.
Missions set population, rating, and monument goals.
Buildings and monument crews draw workers from housing.
Monuments such as pyramids need delivered materials and worker crews over in-game years, and many missions require completing them.

name: Pharaoh
summary: An Egyptian city builder on the Caesar III engine in which a yearly Nile flood waters floodplain farms, walkers carry services to housing, five gods must be appeased, and monuments take years of labor and materials.

claims.text: The CDC invited creator James Vaughan to speak in March 2013 about the game's infection model.

core_loop: infect patient zero -> infections spread within and between countries -> earn DNA points -> buy transmission, symptom, and ability evolutions -> severity raises awareness and cure funding -> race to kill everyone before the cure completes
design_notes: James Vaughan's game inverts the epidemic model: the player owns the pathogen's parameters, and humanity's response (awareness, closures, cure research) is the opponent. The tension is between infectivity and severity, because visible symptoms and deaths accelerate the cure, so successful plans spread quietly and then turn lethal. Countries differ by climate and conditions the pathogen must adapt to, and the CDC invited Vaughan to discuss its infection model in 2013, though Ndemic has said it is not on par with scientific models. Evolved adds 10 disease types, 23 scenarios, versus and co-op modes, and a scenario creator with Workshop sharing.

mechanics.note: Infection spreads within countries and between them along travel links, at rates set by the pathogen's transmission traits and each country's conditions, until countries are fully infected and then depopulated.
DNA points buy nodes in three trees (transmission, symptoms, abilities); symptoms raise severity and lethality, and abilities resist climate and drugs.
Once the disease is noticed, countries fund cure research shown as a global progress bar; finishing it ends the run, so the player races to kill before it fills.
Hot, cold, and other national conditions slow a pathogen that lacks the matching resistance evolutions.
Evolved ships 23 scenarios and 10 disease types, each with altered rules.
The Evolved scenario creator builds custom plagues, worlds, and events, with over 10,000 shared on Steam Workshop.

name: Plague Inc.
summary: A strategy game in which the player evolves a pathogen's transmission, symptoms, and abilities to infect and kill the world's population before humanity's cure research finishes.

core_loop: sculpt terrain and build modular scenery -> design coasters and test their ratings -> guests choose rides, shops, and paths -> manage staff, prices, and finances -> share parks and blueprints on the Workshop
design_notes: Planet Coaster keeps the RollerCoaster Tycoon structure of rated rides and guests with preferences and moves the emphasis to construction: a hybrid spline and piece coaster editor, a voxel terrain editor, and modular pieces that snap into custom buildings. The Workshop is part of play, since players import coasters, scenery blueprints, and whole parks made by others. Frontier calls it a spiritual successor to its own RollerCoaster Tycoon 3, and both run on Frontier's Cobra engine. Career, Challenge (limited funds and research), and Sandbox (unlimited funds) modes share one simulation.

mechanics.note: Coasters are built in a hybrid spline and piece-by-piece editor, and structures are assembled from modular wall, roof, and prop pieces.
Coasters are test-run and rated on excitement, fear, and nausea, which set guest demand and ride value.
Thousands of guests with individual needs, preferences, and budgets choose rides and shops and show thoughts about prices and park conditions.
Coasters, scenery blueprints, and parks are uploaded to and downloaded from the Steam Workshop or Frontier Workshop.
Any selection of pieces can be saved as a blueprint and placed again.
Janitors, mechanics, entertainers, vendors, and security guards are hired and assigned.
Ticket, ride, and shop prices are weighed against ride ratings and guest budgets.
Rides age and break down without mechanic inspections.
A voxel terrain editor sculpts and tunnels the ground.
Challenge and Career modes gate rides and items behind research.
Guests need food, drink, toilets, and rest during their visit.
Career scenarios set goals such as building coasters, reaching park ratings, and hiring staff; a scenario editor was added in 2017.
Scenery around rides and paths raises guest happiness and ride appeal.
Coasters are built in a hybrid spline and piece-by-piece editor, joining track elements end to end.

name: Planet Coaster
summary: A 3D theme park builder with a spline and piece coaster editor, modular scenery, and individually simulated guests and staff, built around sharing creations through the Steam Workshop.

core_loop: build a habitat for a species' needs -> animals respond to space, terrain, enrichment, and group size -> breed and manage genomes -> trade or release animals for conservation -> guests pay and learn -> expand the zoo
design_notes: Planet Zoo gives each animal species a requirements profile (habitat size, land and water, terrain and plant biome, temperature, group size and sex ratio, enrichment, privacy, and guest exposure) and reports the shortfalls as welfare, so habitat design is a constraint-satisfaction problem. Each animal carries a genome that affects lifespan, size, health, and fertility; offspring inherit it, and inbreeding harms the young, which turns breeding into a population-genetics task. Franchise mode connects zoos to an online market where players buy and trade animals with conservation credits. It reuses Planet Coaster's construction and Workshop tools.

mechanics.note: Each species needs habitat size, land and water area, biome terrain and plants, temperature, shelter, and enrichment; welfare drops when any requirement is unmet.
Animals carry genomes that set lifespan, size, health, and fertility; offspring inherit them, and inbreeding causes harmful effects.
Animals have food, water, social, enrichment, and privacy needs whose shortfalls lower welfare and can cause illness.
In Franchise mode an online animal market shared across players lists animals for sale and trade, priced in conservation credits.
A conservation rating rises with endangered species, releases to the wild, and education.
Guests choose exhibits, shops, and talks and react to animal welfare and park layout.
Keepers, vets, mechanics, security, and vendors are hired with work zones and facility needs.
Animals age from juveniles to adults and die of old age.
Barriers, buildings, and scenery use Planet Coaster's modular piece system.
Vets research species to unlock knowledge and enrichment items.
Habitat and building blueprints are shared on the Steam Workshop.

name: Planet Zoo
summary: A zoo management game where the player builds habitats to meet each species' welfare needs, manages genetics and breeding, and raises a conservation rating, using Planet Coaster's building tools.

core_loop: read anchors, vehicles, and budget -> place beams and roads from materials -> run the simulation -> watch stress and failures -> trim cost or reinforce -> submit to leaderboard
design_notes: Bridges are trusses of joints and members in a side-view plane; each material (road, wood, steel, rope, cable, hydraulics) has its own cost, strength, and mass, and crossing vehicles load the structure until members exceed their limit and snap. The puzzle is minimizing cost under a level budget while keeping stress below breaking, and hydraulic phases tied to vehicle checkpoints let bridges move in sync with traffic. Failed runs are free to repeat, so the loop is fast iteration against a stress readout.

mechanics.note: Every member carries tension or compression shown as a stress color; a member past its material limit breaks and the load redistributes, often cascading into collapse.
Bridges are built from road, wood, steel, rope, cable, and hydraulic members connected at joints; materials trade cost against strength and weight.
A level passes when its vehicles reach their flags; total material cost against the level budget is the measure of a good solution, and Steam leaderboards compare results.
Cars, trucks, and other vehicles are physics bodies whose mass and speed load the bridge.
Levels fix anchor points, allowed materials, budget, and vehicle routes.
A multi-phase hydraulics controller fires pistons when vehicles reach checkpoints.
Sandbox designs are published as Workshop levels, and test runs export as GIF replays.

name: Poly Bridge
summary: A bridge-building puzzle game where the player places beams and roads from materials with different costs and strengths under a budget, then runs a physics test as vehicles cross.

core_loop: raise and lower land to make flat ground -> followers settle and build houses -> houses breed followers and raise mana -> spend mana on knights, earthquakes, swamps, volcanoes, and floods -> overwhelm the rival deity's followers
design_notes: Populous established the god game by making terrain the player's main tool and population the player's currency: flat land lets followers build larger houses, houses produce followers, and followers produce mana for powers, so shaping the land is also running the economy. The landscape type of each world (desert, lava, snow and ice) changes how followers develop. Population growth from housing has no mechanic id yet (proposal filed). The game ships 500 worlds, each won by outgrowing and destroying the opposing population.

mechanics.note: Raising and lowering land is the basic power; its main use is creating flat ground on which followers can build larger settlements.
Mana from the follower population unlocks progressively stronger interventions: knights, earthquakes, swamps, volcanoes, and floods.
A papal magnet and behavior modes send followers to settle, gather, or fight.
Landscape type changes how followers develop.
500 worlds, each won by defeating the enemy's followers.

name: Populous
summary: The first god game, in which the player raises and lowers land so followers can build and multiply, then spends the mana they generate on disasters against a rival deity's people.

core_loop: accept a job -> pick nozzle and soap -> wash surfaces -> per-part progress reaches 100 percent -> job pays -> buy washer upgrades -> next job
design_notes: The simulation is a per-surface dirt state: each surface carries layers (dirt, grime, lichen, moss, rust) that the spray removes according to nozzle, soap, and range, and every object reports its percentage done. Four nozzles trade power against spray width, so play is matching the tool to the layer and distance. Progress bars per object and a highlight for remaining dirt make completion fully legible, and the career's story arrives as client text messages rather than through the simulation.

mechanics.note: Four nozzles with different power and spray width and surface-specific soaps remove dirt, grime, lichen, moss, and rust; progress bars track each object and the level, and a button highlights remaining dirt.
Career mode in the town of Muckingham offers 38 main jobs plus bonus jobs whose pay buys upgrades and cosmetics.
Ladders and scaffolding reach higher surfaces.
Challenge mode limits water or time and ranks the result.

name: PowerWash Simulator
summary: A first-person cleaning sim in which the player power-washes vehicles and buildings, choosing nozzles and soaps to strip dirt layers until every part reports clean.

core_loop: set three activity periods for the month -> training and jobs change attributes, money, and fatigue -> events and festivals test her attributes -> rest or vacation to prevent illness -> she ages a year -> at 18 her attributes select a career ending
design_notes: Takami Akai designed the sequel to answer complaints that the original was repetitive, adding more reactions and events around a schedule-and-attributes core. Each month splits into early, middle, and late periods, each assigned to training (academic, artistic, religious, military, or magical), a part-time job, adventure, or free time, under a small annual income. Jobs unlock with age and pay promotion and streak bonuses, rival girls age alongside the daughter as benchmarks, and October festivals hold contests in martial arts, dance, art, and cooking. At 18 her attributes and history select one of 74 career endings, a branching-outcome model captured by the care-dependent-development mechanic.

mechanics.note: Training courses and part-time jobs raise and lower her attributes; attributes gate jobs, decide October festival contests in martial arts, dance, art, and cooking against rival girls, and select the final career.
Each month has three activity slots (early, middle, late), so every period spent training, working, adventuring, or resting is a period not spent on the others.
The daughter ages from 10 to 18; jobs and events unlock with age, and the game ends at 18.
Repeating a part-time job leads to promotions, higher pay, and bonuses for unbroken success streaks.
Stress from work and training is relieved by free time, vacations, spa stays, or bed rest; poor rest management leads to illness and weaker performance.
A small annual income pays for lessons, clothing, food, treatment, and shopping; jobs supplement it.
The month is the turn, split into three phases that resolve after the player sets the schedule.
Events and reactions fire on age, attributes, and season, leading into 74 career endings with retrospective sequences.
Eight years of scheduled training, jobs, and rest shape the daughter's attributes, and at 18 her attributes and history select one of 74 career endings.

name: Princess Maker 2
summary: A raising sim in which the player, as a father figure, schedules a daughter's training, part-time jobs, rest, and adventures from age 10 to 18, and her accumulated attributes decide one of 74 endings.

core_loop: build cells, canteens, and yards -> set the hourly regime -> prisoners pursue needs within the schedule -> unmet needs raise misconduct, contraband, and riots -> hire staff, run programs, and claim grants -> expand capacity for more prisoners and income
design_notes: Control is indirect: the player cannot order prisoners, only shape the regime, the buildings that satisfy each need, and the staff who enforce rules. Each of about 21 needs is a charge from 1 to 10 satisfied by specific objects for set durations (a phone booth takes 25 minutes, a shower 20), and needs left at the top charge produce side effects. Information itself is a staffed system: features such as viewing finances unlock only after hiring the matching staff member, such as an accountant. Prisoners fall into five security levels with different temperaments, sentence lengths, and cashflow, and reform and labor programs reduce recidivism, which feeds the prison's grade.

mechanics.note: About 21 prisoner needs (bladder, food, sleep, hygiene, freedom, family, privacy, spirituality, and others) each charge from 1 to 10 and are reset by specific objects or activities; a need at 10 triggers its side effect, and reports color needs from green to red.

Hiring a Warden unlocks an hourly regime per risk category with Lockup, Sleep, Eat, Yard, Shower, Free Time, and Work blocks; each block confines prisoners to areas rather than forcing actions, so needs are met only where the current block lets prisoners go.
The prison is drawn tile by tile: foundations, walls, doors, and objects are placed, then workmen build them, and room types are assigned to enclosed areas that contain required objects.
Needs left unmet for long periods make prisoners irritated, then likely to fight, attack staff, attempt escape, or riot, and violence spreads to nearby prisoners until guards restore order.
Guards, dog handlers, armed guards, and snitches counter contraband, gangs, and escape attempts through patrols, searches, and lockdowns.
Income per prisoner per day against staff wages and construction.
Staff such as guards, cooks, janitors, doctors, psychologists, and lawyers are hired individually, and administrators unlock features.
A bureaucracy research tree unlocked through administrative staff.
Federal grants pay out for meeting stated construction or program objectives.
Five security levels with different temperaments, sentence lengths, and cashflow, plus death row.
Crowd flow through doors and corridors shapes congestion and fights.
Generators and cables power doors, lights, and kitchens.
Water pumps and pipes supply showers and toilets.
Fires spread through the prison and must be fought by firemen.
Player prisons are shared online, and Escape Mode lets players break out of shared prisons.

name: Prison Architect
summary: A prison management sim in which the player builds a facility, sets an hourly regime, and staffs it while hundreds of prisoners pursue needs whose neglect leads to fights, escapes, and riots.

core_loop: sign insurer contracts -> patients arrive with complaints -> doctors order examinations and lab tests -> revealed symptoms narrow the diagnosis -> treat, hospitalize, or operate -> insurers pay -> build departments and hire staff
design_notes: Oxymoron Games reduced medicine to symptom rules: each diagnosis has symptoms with tuned occurrence frequencies, examinations reveal them, and a diagnosis becomes clear once enough are found; frequencies were set so a case is rarely obvious after the first exam. Patients reach the hospital through insurance company contracts, and the developers say the resulting economy came to resemble the American system. The free Doctor Mode update lets the player make individual doctors' exam and treatment choices, turning the facility sim into a diagnosis game.

mechanics.note: Each patient has a hidden diagnosis; doctors order examinations, lab tests, and equipment procedures that each reveal symptoms, symptom frequencies are tuned so one exam rarely settles a case, and treatment, hospitalization, or surgery follows.
The player hires and specializes doctors, nurses, lab staff, and janitors and manages their job satisfaction; the Hospital Services DLC adds staff training.
The player lays foundations, walls, floor tiles, doors, and windows and places equipment for each department, or starts from prefabs.
Doctor Mode (2019) lets the player choose exams, diagnoses, and treatments for individual doctors and their patients.
A campaign and six challenge levels set goals; sandbox mode removes them.

name: Project Hospital
summary: A hospital management sim in which the player builds departments and hires staff while doctors diagnose patients by ordering examinations that reveal symptoms until one diagnosis remains.

claims.text: Experiments ranged from 10 to 500 agents in reported results; runs above 1,000 agents were attempted but exceeded the Minecraft server's capacity.

core_loop: seed agents with personas and community goals -> concurrent modules perceive, remember, talk, and act in Minecraft -> cognitive controller commits a coherent decision -> roles specialize and rules are paid, debated, and amended -> beliefs and memes spread between towns
design_notes: PIANO runs about ten modules concurrently at different speeds (memory, action awareness, goal generation, social awareness, talking, skill execution), with fast non-language reflex networks and a cognitive controller that acts as a bottleneck and broadcasts one decision so speech and action stay consistent; GPT-4o was the strongest base model. In 30-agent runs agents settled into persistent roles (farmer, miner, engineer, guard, explorer, blacksmith) that collapsed without the social module. In a 29-agent constitution experiment with a 20 percent tax paid into community chests every 120 seconds, pro- and anti-tax influencers shifted votes, amendments passed, and payments followed the new rate. In a 500-agent run, Pastafarianism seeded by 20 priests spread to other towns; 1,000-agent attempts exceeded the Minecraft server's capacity. The preprint states no public code release.

mechanics.note: Constituents give feedback on a constitution, amendments are generated, agents vote, and the amended constitution is distributed on a fixed schedule (feedback at 300 s, vote at 420 s, distribution at 600 s).

Agents deposit a share of inventory into community chests every 120 seconds at the constitutional rate, starting at 20 percent; when amendments cut it to 5-10 percent, payments fell to about 9 percent.
Memes and a religion (Pastafarianism, seeded by 20 priests in one town) spread through agent conversations and travel; conversion was tracked by keyword use and had not saturated after two hours.
A memory module stores conversations, actions, and observations across short and long timescales.
A social-awareness module infers other agents' sentiment, and the paper compares perceived with true likeability.
Agents gather and craft Minecraft items; a 49-agent group plateaued at about 320 unique items over four hours.
Goal generation, talking, and the cognitive controller run on language-model calls, with GPT-4o as the base model in the strongest configuration.

name: Project Sid
summary: An Altera research demonstration that runs 10 to 1,000-plus language-model agents with the concurrent PIANO architecture in Minecraft to study role specialization, collective rule-making, and cultural transmission.

core_loop: loot houses and stores -> avoid or fight zombies drawn by sight and noise -> manage hunger, fatigue, injuries, and moodles -> utilities fail and seasons turn -> barricade, farm, and level skills -> survive until death
design_notes: The framing question is how the character dies, not whether: zombie infection is always fatal in an unmodified game, so play is about extending a doomed run. Water and power shut off within the first month, after which erosion and overgrowth spread, giving the sandbox a scheduled decline. Zombies respond to sight and hearing and hordes migrate, so noise from actions shapes risk; there is no mechanic id for noise attraction yet (proposal filed). The game has been in early access since a paid tech demo in May 2011, with Steam early access from November 2013 and Build 42 in open beta from December 2024.

mechanics.note: Moodles for hunger, thirst, fatigue, endurance, panic, stress, boredom, unhappiness, temperature, wetness, pain, bleeding, and sickness each grow in severity and penalize combat, movement, carrying, or healing.
Wounds such as scratches, lacerations, bites, and fractures are tracked per body part with bleeding and bandaging; zombie infection is spread by saliva and blood and is always fatal.
Skills such as carpentry and cooking level from activities, and skill books and magazines speed or unlock progress.
Water and power shut off within about a month, forcing preparation.
Occupation and positive or negative traits are chosen at character creation; occupation also sets spawn location.
Weapons, tools, and barricades are crafted; Build 42 overhauled crafting.
Carpentry builds walls, barricades, and forts.
A climate system with seasons changes gear needs.
Food rots, and refrigeration ends when power fails.
Vehicles have physics and part condition.
A vision cone limits what the survivor sees.
Death ends the character; a new survivor can start in the same world.
Full Lua modding through the Steam Workshop.
Zombies respond to sight and hearing, so noise from actions such as gunfire or breaking windows draws them toward the survivor, and hordes migrate.

name: Project Zomboid
summary: An isometric zombie survival sandbox in which one survivor manages moodles, injuries, skills, and failing utilities across a large Kentucky map until an inevitable death.

core_loop: pick a level goal -> choose an initiator, a target, and a social exchange -> rules score volition and acceptance -> relationships, statuses, and history update -> new exchanges open -> the goal is met or the story turns another way
design_notes: Prom Week runs on Comme il Faut (CiF), which its UCSC authors describe as making social relationships playable: characters have traits, interests, statuses, and directed networks of liking, attraction, and respect, and more than 5,000 social considerations govern what each character wants and how others respond. The player never writes dialogue but chooses which social exchange a character initiates; CiF offers the exchanges a character is inclined toward, ranked by likelihood, and resolves acceptance from the social state of everyone involved, including what third parties think. Levels set story goals such as getting two characters to date, which turns the rule base into a puzzle with many solutions.
developer: UC Santa Cruz Expressive Intelligence Studio

mechanics.note: Exchanges such as winking, being friendly, or being mean have preconditions; CiF rules decide whether the target accepts and update networks and statuses.
Directed social networks track how much each character likes, is attracted to, and respects each other character; exchanges and third parties' opinions move the values.
A character's volition for each exchange is scored from matching rules, and only exchanges it is inclined toward are offered, ranked by likelihood.
Traits and interests weight which rules apply to a character.
Past exchanges are stored as social history that later rules reference.
Each level sets social goals, such as getting two named characters to date.

name: Prom Week
summary: A 2012 browser social sim in which the player picks social exchanges among 18 high school students in the week before prom, with the Comme il Faut rule system deciding who wants to do what and how targets respond.

core_loop: lay track and place stations -> buy trains and set consists and stops -> carry cargo to stations where it is demanded -> revenue and industry growth -> raise capital through bonds and stock -> defend against rival barons
design_notes: Railroad Tycoon joins a train-operations model to a corporate-finance model. Stations come in four sizes (signal tower, depot, station, terminal) with growing service areas, and an economy setting chooses between a simple economy where big cities buy almost anything and a complex one where they buy only certain goods. The company starts with $1 million split between equity and a loan, raises more through bonds, and trades in a small stock market where rival barons attempt buyouts and rate wars. Meier took the idea from the board game 1830 and also cited SimCity. Track construction has no matching mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as track-laying), and dated vehicle availability is proposed as dated-tech-timeline.

mechanics.note: Each train gets ordered stops and a consist of mail, passenger, and freight cars for nine commodity types; consists can be changed at any stop.
Stations supply and demand goods and passengers; under the complex economy cities accept only certain products, so routing follows demand.
A small stock market lets the player trade its own and rival stock; rivals use stock dealings to try to take over the player's railroad.
AI railroad barons build competing lines and start rate wars over shared stations.
Track is laid on a square tile grid and up to 32 stations are placed; the first station gets the engine shop where trains are built.
Depots, stations, and terminals draw cargo from progressively larger surrounding areas.
Signal towers act as passing loops and control train movements on shared track.
Industries consume delivered freight and produce new cargo; players can build additional industries.
Starting capital is half a loan; bonds raise more at interest rates tied to the economy.
Accounts settle in two-year periods across a century of play.
Players can take direct control of individual train movements.
Delivery revenue depends on cargo type, distance, and travel time, so fast trains earn more for passengers and mail.
New locomotive types become available as the calendar advances through the eras, from early steam engines toward diesels.
Track is laid tile by tile across terrain whose slope and features add cost, linking up to 32 stations.

name: Railroad Tycoon
summary: A railroad business sim in which the player lays track, builds stations, schedules trains to meet regional supply and demand, and battles rival barons through the stock market.

core_loop: fund civilian initiatives in regions -> popular support rises -> spending raises corruption and inflation -> an insurgency emerges and contests regions -> deploy troops, counter corruption, or negotiate -> stabilize the country to win
design_notes: Rebel Inc. inverts Ndemic's earlier Plague Inc.: instead of spreading a disease, the player contains an insurgency by building popular support, and spending itself generates corruption and inflation. The tension is between civilian initiatives that win support slowly and military spending that holds ground without building support. Corruption as a side effect of spending is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal corruption-leakage).

mechanics.note: A monthly budget funds infrastructure, jobs, education, roads, and military spending; the more initiatives the player funds, the more corruption and inflation rise, and the Economist governor receives the whole budget annually.
An insurgency emerges partway through and contests regions against coalition forces; later, peace can be negotiated with insurgent leaders.
Civilian initiatives raise popular support region by region, and stabilizing the country without letting insurgents take control is the goal.
A governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.
Random events interrupt plans and offer choices.
