Each region has its own geography, and selectable governors such as the Economist and the Warlord change the rules.
Funding more civilian initiatives raises corruption and inflation, which erode what the monthly budget achieves; the governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.

name: Rebel Inc.
summary: A counterinsurgency strategy game in which the player, as a coalition governor, spends a monthly budget on civilian and military initiatives to build popular support and stabilize regions of a war-torn country while corruption, inflation, and an insurgency push back.

core_loop: draw an adviser's card -> swipe left or right -> church, people, army, and treasury meters shift -> a meter hits empty or full -> the king dies -> the next reign begins with unlocked cards
design_notes: Reigns reduces governance to four bounded meters in which both extremes are fatal, so every choice is a balancing act rather than a maximization. The swipe interface, modeled on Tinder, keeps each decision binary and fast. It is a boundary case included for the dilemma-card mechanic and its use of death as progress between reigns.

mechanics.note: Advisers present cards that the player swipes left or right; each choice moves one or more of four meters (church, people, army, treasury), and the reign ends when any meter becomes completely full or completely empty.
When a king's reign ends, play continues with a new king; unlocked cards and some effects carry across reigns, and the in-game years keep advancing.
Story cards chain across reigns, such as the Devil's visits in the years 666, 1332, and 1998.
Completing tasks unlocks new cards.

name: Reigns
summary: A swipe-based card game in which the player, as a succession of medieval monarchs, accepts or rejects advisers' requests that push church, people, army, and treasury meters, and each reign ends when any meter empties or fills.

core_loop: designate work -> colonists self-assign by priority -> needs and moods shift -> storyteller injects events -> colony adapts or collapses
design_notes: Tynan Sylvester describes RimWorld as a story generator. Its systems are chosen for how legible and story-relevant their outputs are rather than for realism: thoughts are itemized with sources and durations, injuries are named body parts, and raids scale with colony wealth to keep tension.

mechanics.note: Selectable storytellers (Cassandra, Phoebe, Randy) choose incidents using a threat budget derived from colony wealth and time since the last major event.
Colonists track food, rest, recreation, comfort, beauty, and other needs whose levels feed mood.
Mood below trait-adjusted break thresholds triggers minor, major, or extreme mental breaks; high mood can grant inspirations.
Every mood effect is an itemized thought with a source and expiry, visible in the needs tab.
A work tab matrix sets 1-4 priorities per colonist per job type; colonists self-assign.
Bodies are hierarchies of parts with hit points, bleeding, infection, scars, and prosthetics that change capacities like moving and manipulation.
Raid strength scales with colony wealth, number of colonists, and difficulty, so growth raises danger.
Drafting switches a colonist from self-assigned work to direct player control for combat or emergencies.

name: RimWorld
summary: A colony sim where a few named colonists with needs, traits, injuries, and relationships survive on a frontier planet while a storyteller AI paces events.

core_loop: build paths, rides, and shops -> design coasters and test their ratings -> guests choose rides by intensity preference and budget -> thoughts reveal problems -> adjust prices, staff, and layout -> meet the scenario goal
design_notes: RollerCoaster Tycoon makes ride design measurable: every built ride is test-run and rated on excitement, intensity, and nausea, and each guest has a preferred intensity and a nausea tolerance, so the ratings decide who will ride and who gets sick afterward. Guests are individual agents with money, needs, and a stream of readable thoughts, which makes park problems inspectable one guest at a time. Rides lose reliability with age and break down unless mechanics inspect them on a player-set interval. Scenario goals (guest counts and park rating by a deadline) chain 21 base parks. OpenRCT2, a reimplementation of RCT2, carries the systems forward, and Planet Coaster and Parkitect are described as spiritual successors.

mechanics.note: Each ride is test-run and rated on excitement, intensity, and nausea from its track geometry, speeds, and g-forces; ratings set demand and fair price.
Guests have money, a preferred ride intensity, a nausea tolerance, and needs, and they report thoughts such as a ride being too intense or a price too high.
Coasters are built track piece by piece on a tile grid, choosing direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews.
Guests compare ride and shop prices with ride value and their remaining cash; overpriced items show up as complaints in guest thoughts.
Ride reliability decays with use and age; breakdown chance rises as reliability falls, and mechanics inspect and repair on a set interval.
Handymen sweep, empty bins, and mow; mechanics fix rides; security guards prevent vandalism; entertainers cheer guests.
Clicking a guest shows cash, needs, thoughts, and ride history.
Guests get hungry, thirsty, tired, and need toilets during a visit.
Guests wait in ride queues and leave long lines unhappy.
Land can be raised and lowered and water added to fit rides and add appeal.
Each of 21 base scenarios sets a goal such as a guest count with a minimum park rating by a deadline; completing one unlocks the next.
Paid research unlocks new rides and improvements over time.
Scenery and trees improve guest views and ride appeal.
Parks start with a loan, such as $50,000 in Mega Park.
Guests navigate the path network and can get lost in mazes of paths.

The marketing panel runs time-limited paid campaigns, such as park or ride advertising and free-entry or half-price vouchers, that raise guest arrivals or demand for a chosen ride or stall while they last.
Coaster track is built piece by piece on the tile grid by direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews, and the result is rated by test run.

name: RollerCoaster Tycoon
summary: An amusement park management game in which the player builds rides and custom coasters piece by piece, rated for excitement, intensity, and nausea, to satisfy guests with individual preferences and meet scenario goals.

claims.text: Press coverage compares Satisfactory's building to Factorio, and the game is widely treated as a 3D first-person take on Factorio's factory loop; the cited source records the comparison rather than a developer statement of influence.

core_loop: scout resource nodes -> place miners -> belt ore through smelters, constructors, and assemblers -> deliver parts to the HUB and Space Elevator -> unlock the next tier -> expand power and logistics to distant nodes
design_notes: Satisfactory moves the Factorio-style ratio puzzle into a hand-built 3D world explored on foot, so verticality, foundations, and architecture become part of layout and many players build for appearance as well as throughput. Resource nodes never deplete and are graded impure, normal, or pure (0.5x, 1x, 2x), so expansion is driven by needing more node types and output rather than by exhaustion. The power grid fails as a whole: when demand exceeds supply and storage is empty the fuse trips and every connected building stops until the player resets it, unlike grids that slow machines proportionally. Clock speed (1% to 250%, with Power Shards and a power exponent of about 1.32) and 106 alternate recipes from crash-site hard drives give each factory a recipe-selection layer that the taxonomy folds into production-chain; this run proposed a machine-boosting mechanic for clock speed and similar systems, and a megaproject-sink mechanic for the Space Elevator. There are no base-raiding enemies; fauna threaten only the pioneer.

mechanics.note: Smelters, constructors, assemblers, manufacturers, refineries, and blenders run per-minute recipes; 106 alternate recipes chosen from hard-drive scans swap inputs, and clock speed from 1% to 250% rescales any machine.
Six belt tiers carry 60, 120, 270, 480, 780, and 1,200 items per minute, with splitters, mergers, lifts, and smart splitters routing flows in 3D.
Miners Mk.1 to Mk.3 sit on infinite ore nodes whose purity multiplies output by 0.5, 1, or 2; water extractors, oil extractors, and resource well pressurizers tap fluids.
Generators from 30 MW biomass burners to 2,500 MW nuclear plants feed one grid; if consumption exceeds production with storage empty, the fuse trips and all connected buildings stop until reset.
HUB milestones are unlocked by delivering crafted parts tier by tier, Space Elevator phases gate tiers 3 to 9, and the MAM researches alien items, power slugs, and hard drives.
The pioneer walks, jetpacks, ziplines, and drives across a hand-built map, building only within reach and gathering power slugs, hard drives, and samples on foot.
Foundations, walls, and ramps snap to a grid at any height, so factories are stacked floors connected by belt lifts and pipes.
Pipelines carry 300 or 600 m3 per minute; liquids need head lift supplied by pumps, while gases do not.
Trains follow station timetables, trucks and tractors replay recorded routes, and drones shuttle between a home port and one linked port on battery or packaged fuel.
Block and path signals divide track so several trains can share a network.
A Blueprint Designer (40 x 40 m at Mk.1, larger tiers in 1.0) saves layouts that appear as build-menu entries and draw materials from storage or inventory.
Storage containers, fluid buffers, and industrial tanks buffer production; the Dimensional Depot uploads items for remote building.
Refinery recipes emit heavy oil residue or polymer resin that must be routed or the line backs up, and nuclear plants emit waste that has to be stored or reprocessed.
Early parts are crafted at a craft bench by holding a button, and equipment is made at the equipment workshop.
The community-run Satisfactory Mod Loader adds new buildings, recipes, and logic on top of the Unreal Engine game.

The Space Elevator takes five Project Assembly phases of crafted parts, from 50 Smart Plating in phase 1 to Nuclear Pasta and Ballistic Warp Drives in phase 5, and its phases unlock tiers 3 to 9 and the ending.
Clock speed from 1% to 250% rescales any machine; each of up to three Power Shards raises the cap by 50 points, and power scales with exponent about 1.32, so 250% draws about 336% of base power.
Trucks and tractors replay a route the player records by driving it once, stopping at truck stations along the recorded path.

name: Satisfactory
summary: A first-person 3D factory automation game in which a pioneer taps infinite resource nodes on an alien planet and connects machines with belts, pipes, trains, and drones to deliver project parts to FICSIT's Space Elevator.

core_loop: grow or cook a base product -> mix in ingredients to add effects -> sell to customers who want those effects -> avoid police searches and curfews -> hire dealers and staff -> buy properties -> unlock new regions
design_notes: Schedule I runs a production business through a first-person avatar: the player waters plants, operates mixing and cooking stations, and walks or drives deals across Hyland Point before hiring dealers, botanists, cooks, and janitors to automate the chain. Mixing common ingredients such as soft drinks or paracetamol into a product adds effects that raise its sale value, and customers want particular effects, so recipe discovery is the product-development layer. Police pressure rises with growth through random searches, roadblocks, and curfews, and being seen breaking the law sets a wanted status, a player-heat rule the taxonomy lacks (proposed as heat-wanted-level). The game is in early access, with an exit planned for Q4 2027.

mechanics.note: Mixing ingredients such as soft drinks or paracetamol into a base product adds named effects that raise its value and match customer preferences.
Customers have preferred effects and price tolerances; matching them builds repeat orders and relationships that open further customers.
Plants are grown in pots with soil and water over a growth timer, then harvested as the base product.
The player personally grows, cooks, mixes, and delivers in first person until staff take over.
Dealers sell to their own customer lists for a cut, and botanists, cooks, and janitors run production at owned properties.
Police pressure grows with operations through patrols, random searches, roadblocks, and night curfews; being seen raises a wanted status that can end in arrest.
Higher products need multi-step chains such as cooking methamphetamine at chemistry stations.
Product quality varies with inputs such as soil and additives and affects price.
A daily clock with a night curfew shapes when deals can be made.
Grow tents, stations, and storage are placed inside bought properties.
Rank and story progress unlock new regions, customers, and equipment.

name: Schedule I
summary: A first-person crime business sim in which the player grows and cooks drugs, mixes ingredients to create products with effects customers want, sells them around a city under police pressure, and automates production with hired staff.

claims.text: In late 2014 Screeps was publicly playable in its browser Simulation mode during its Indiegogo campaign, and a December 2015 post dates the initial launch a year earlier; the persistent MMO opened to backers in May 2015, and the Steam full release followed on 2016-11-16. `year` records the 2014 public launch.

core_loop: write and commit JavaScript -> each tick the script reads room state and issues orders -> creeps harvest energy for spawns, extensions, and the controller -> controller levels unlock structures -> claim and defend rooms against other players' code -> profile and rewrite code within the CPU limit
design_notes: Screeps removes direct control entirely: the only input to the persistent world is the player's main module, which the server runs once per tick against a fixed snapshot, queuing commands that resolve together at tick end, so the colony keeps acting while the player is offline. Computation is the scarce resource: each tick has a CPU limit (20 without CPU Unlock, otherwise rising with Global Control Level to 300), with unused CPU banked in a 10,000-unit bucket that allows bursts of up to 500. Creeps are designed in code as bodies of up to 50 parts (WORK, CARRY, MOVE, ATTACK, RANGED_ATTACK, HEAL, CLAIM, TOUGH) that set cost, ability, and fatigue, and they die after 1,500 ticks, so a colony is a replacement pipeline. Room Controller Levels 1 to 8 unlock structures and decay if not fed energy, and every player's AI meets the others in shared 50x50 rooms, so strategy is emergent competition between programs. The server is open source and runnable privately.

mechanics.note: Players write JavaScript (or C, C++, Rust, Go, C#, and others via WebAssembly) whose main loop runs every tick under a per-tick CPU limit with a 10,000-unit bucket; globals reset between ticks and actions resolve together at tick end.
Official shards run continuously with ticks every 2 to 5 seconds, so colonies harvest, build, and fight while their owners are offline; rooms link through exits and shards through portals.

Code spawns creeps from up to 50 body parts of eight types; part counts set harvest, carry, attack, and heal rates, MOVE parts offset fatigue of 1, 2, or 10 per part on road, plain, or swamp, and each part has 100 hits.
WORK parts harvest energy from sources that refill every 300 ticks, and extractors at RCL 6 mine minerals for labs and the market.

Energy spent on a room controller raises its level from 1 to 8 at cumulative costs up to 10.9 million, unlocking spawns, extensions, towers, storage, links, labs, terminal, factory, observer, and nuker; unfed controllers downgrade and become neutral.
Towers, ramparts, and walls defend rooms against other players and NPC invaders, and a newly placed first spawn grants safe mode.
Terminals post public buy and sell orders priced in credits with a 5% order fee; the party executing a deal pays an energy cost that grows with distance, and NPC terminals sit at highway crossroads.
Movement costs are 1 on roads, 2 on plains, and 10 on swamps, and route searches consume the player's CPU, so caching paths is a core optimization.
Roads and other structures lose hits over time and must be repaired by creeps.
Every creep dies after 1,500 ticks, so code must schedule replacements before roles go unfilled.
The open-source private server supports mods and community servers that change rules and tick rates.

Each tick has a CPU limit (20 without CPU Unlock), unused CPU banks in a bucket of up to 10,000, a tick may burst to 500, and scripts are terminated at the limit, so pathfinding and caching strategies are shaped by CPU cost.

name: Screeps
summary: A persistent MMO strategy game in which players control colonies only by writing JavaScript that the server runs every tick, directing creeps assembled from body parts to harvest energy, upgrade room controllers, trade, and fight other players' code under a CPU budget.

core_loop: check the tank each real day -> adjust heat, clean water, and feed -> talk to Seaman through the microphone -> it learns words and asks about the player -> the life stage advances through breeding and die-off -> raise the Frogman generation and release it
design_notes: Yoot Saito built Seaman around speech: a microphone accessory lets the player answer questions and make small talk, early Gillmen repeat the player's words back as gibberish, and the creature's vocabulary grows while it keeps insulting the player. The care loop is sparse but strict, with roughly one check per real day needed to keep it alive, so the game paces itself to the player's calendar. Its life cycle is scripted and harsh: Gillmen fight until two remain, Podfish die after mating, Tadmen eat each other until two remain, and the final Frogmen are released into the wild. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version as a guide who explains only part of the rules.

mechanics.note: The player sets tank heat, cleans dirty water, and supplies food, and later runs a sprinkler to keep Frogmen moist.
Microphone speech is matched against the creature's current vocabulary; it asks for the player's birthday and other details and answers in conversation.
Mushroomer, Gillman, Podfish, Tadman, and Frogman stages; Podfish parents die after mating and the aquarium becomes a terrarium.
Time follows the real calendar; going much longer than a day without a check can kill the creature.
Vocabulary grows through conversation, and the creature becomes tamer over time.
It remembers facts the player shares, such as a birthday, and later tells historical events from that date.
Tank temperature and water cleanliness must suit the current life stage.
A neglected creature dies permanently.

name: Seaman
summary: A Dreamcast virtual pet in which the player talks through a microphone to a sardonic human-faced fish, managing its tank's heat, water, and food while it matures through five life stages.

core_loop: customize an avatar -> buy or rent land in a region -> build objects from prims and mesh -> script behavior in LSL -> sell creations, land, or services for Linden Dollars -> exchange Linden Dollars on the LindeX
design_notes: Linden Lab describes Second Life as a platform rather than a game: it has no set objective, and almost all content is built and scripted by residents, who keep copyright to it. It is a boundary case included for its user-content pipeline, server-side object scripting, and a virtual currency with a real-money exchange that produced real income for some residents. Each region is simulated on its own CPU core with Havok physics, which caps how many avatars and objects a place can hold.

mechanics.note: The world is a grid of 256 by 256 meter regions, each simulated on a dedicated CPU core with Havok physics and capped at 40 avatars on the mainland or 100 on private islands.
Objects run Linden Scripting Language scripts on Linden Lab's servers, which is how built objects become interactive.
Residents trade land, goods, and services for Linden Dollars, which are bought and sold for real currency on the LindeX exchange; the Marketplace has listed about 2.1 million items.
Objects are built from linked primitives, up to 256 per linked set, or from imported mesh.
Creators keep copyright to their content and sell it to other residents.
Groups give residents shared chat and voice channels.

name: Second Life
summary: A persistent 3D virtual world in which residents build objects from prims and meshes, script them in the Linden Scripting Language, own land in server-simulated regions, and trade goods and land for Linden Dollars exchangeable for real currency.

claims.text: shapez 2 is the sequel to Shapez (2020, also known as shapez.io), which has no entry in this dataset, so the lineage is recorded here rather than as an influenced_by edge.
Early access began on 2024-08-15 and version 1.0 released on 2026-04-23.

core_loop: read the requested shape code -> extract raw shapes from asteroids -> cut, rotate, stack, and paint on belts across levels -> deliver to the Vortex -> earn platform units and research -> build bigger platforms and train networks
design_notes: shapez 2 removes enemies, money, and building costs (all buildings are free) and keeps only the throughput puzzle: the product is an abstract shape of up to four layers of four quadrants, each part with a type and one of nine colors, written as a shape code. Parts obey a support rule (no floating pieces) and crystals shatter when cut from or stacked onto other crystals, so processing order is part of the puzzle. Space is the scarce resource: machines sit on space platforms whose count is limited by Platform Units earned from goals, and platforms connect through edge notches, space belts, and colored train lines whose routing is set per color at splitters. After the fixed milestones, operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level (for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth), turning the endgame into scaling a design rather than designing a new one.

mechanics.note: Cutters, rotators, stackers, swappers, painters, pin pushers, and crystal generators each transform shapes by fixed rules; a target shape code implies a processing sequence the player must lay out.
Belts, splitters, mergers, and lifts move shapes across three building levels per platform, and space belts carry them between platforms.

Delivering each milestone's required shapes to the Vortex unlocks the next buildings and mechanics, such as fluids, painting, crystals, and trains; afterwards, operator goal lines with exponentially rising shape costs reward platform units, blueprint points, and research points.
Space platforms in 20x20 chunks are the limited building surface, capped by Platform Units, with notches at chunk edges as the only connection points between platforms.
Copying and pasting factory sections costs Blueprint Points earned from goals, making repeated modules the intended way to scale.
Each platform has three stacked building levels, and shapes carry up to four or five vertical layers that must be supported from below.

Space trains load fixed-size packages at loader stations and unload at stops; each rail carries trains of several colors that take their own color's branch at splitters, and wagons hold one package per machine level.
Pipes and space pipes carry fluids such as paint from asteroid pumps to painters, and fluid launchers move them across notches.
Wire machines carry signals that read and control machines, and wireless senders and receivers pass signals across platform notches.
Asteroid miners and pumps on platforms extract raw shape fields and fluid deposits from a procedurally generated world.
Mods load natively through the ShapezShifter API and are distributed on Steam Workshop.
After the fixed milestones, operator goal lines at the Vortex demand shapes in quantities that grow exponentially per level (for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth), absorbing late-game output.

name: shapez 2
summary: A combat-free factory automation game in which the player builds multi-level factories on space platforms that cut, rotate, stack, and paint layered geometric shapes and deliver them to a central Vortex to meet escalating milestone and operator goals.

core_loop: receive a patrol grid -> transit under time compression -> detect contacts -> identify the target and solve speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle -> fire torpedoes -> evade escorts -> return to base and promote crew
design_notes: The campaign engine generates convoys, destroyer escorts, and task forces in each patrol area rather than scripting engagements, so a career starting between 1939 and 1943 is a sequence of unplanned encounters. Realism settings scale the procedure: at the hardest, the player identifies class and nationality and computes speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle; with manual targeting off a Weapons Officer solves the problem while approach geometry still matters. Crew members persist between patrols with rank, experience, morale, and decorations.

mechanics.note: The campaign engine generates convoys, destroyer escorts, and task forces in assigned patrol grids, and the player chooses targets and approaches.
Manual targeting requires identifying a vessel's class and nationality and computing its speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle before setting torpedo depth and spread.
Crew members carry rank, experience, morale, and decorations between patrols.
A career begins at the rank of Lieutenant, Jr., with a U-boat base assignment between 1939 and 1943.
With manual targeting off, a Weapons Officer computes the firing solution.
Torpedoes run at a set speed, depth, and gyro angle toward an intercept computed from target speed and angle on the bow, so a bad solution misses.

name: Silent Hunter III
summary: A World War II U-boat sim with a dynamic campaign that generates convoys and escorts, manual torpedo targeting, and a persistent crew that gains rank, experience, and morale across patrols.

core_loop: steer the yellow ant -> lay trails and recruit followers to food or the red nest -> colony grows under caste allocation -> fight the red colony and survive hazards -> send young queens and drones to found new nests -> take the yard and drive out the humans
design_notes: Will Wright drew on Hölldobler and Wilson's The Ants to show emergence: individual ants follow simple rules, and the player's main lever on the colony is the trail field that other ants follow, not orders. The player embodies one ant and can swap into any other, which pairs a direct-avatar view with colony-level allocation of workers, soldiers, and breeders. Rain washes away trails and floods nests, and lawnmowers, bug spray, spiders, and antlions kill ants, so the environment erodes the information the player lays down. Trail-following agents are not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal stigmergic-trails).

mechanics.note: The player is one yellow ant that digs, carries food and pebbles, receives food by trophallaxis, and fights; double-clicking another ant moves control to it.
The yellow ant lays trails to food or enemy nests that other black ants follow, and can recruit a group of nearby ants to follow it into fights against spiders, caterpillars, antlions, or red ants.
The colony divides into workers (forage, dig, tend brood), soldiers (fight, eat more, cannot tend brood), the queen, and winged breeders, and the player sets the balance.
The queen lays eggs that become larvae and adults; young queens and drones mate to found colonies in new map squares.
Rain washes away trails and can flood nests.
Human footsteps, lawnmowers, bug spray, and electrical outlets kill ants without warning.
Surface yard play is viewed from above while nests are shown in side view underground.

name: SimAnt
summary: A Maxis ant-colony simulation in which the player controls one yellow ant that lays trails and recruits nestmates while managing a black colony's castes against a rival red colony, predators, and the household.

core_loop: zone residential, commercial, and industrial land -> connect roads and power -> RCI demand and land value grow zones -> collect taxes each year -> fund police, fire, and roads -> respond to crime, pollution, traffic, and disasters
design_notes: Will Wright grew the game out of the map editor he built for Raid on Bungeling Bay and drew its model from Jay Forrester's Urban Dynamics. The simulation is a set of coarse grid maps (land value, crime, pollution, traffic density, police and fire effect) recomputed in passes, plus three RCI demand valves that integrate city-wide balance; a zone grows when its local score plus the valve passes a random test. The 2008 GPL release as Micropolis made these update rules, including crime = 128 - land value + density - police effect, inspectable.

mechanics.note: The player paints 3x3 residential, commercial, and industrial zones; simulated developers build, densify, or abandon them.
Three valves move by the ratio of projected to actual residents, commerce, and industry plus a tax offset, clamped to +/-2000 or +/-1500 (Micropolis source).
Each 2x2 block's value falls with distance from the population-weighted center, rises near trees and water, and drops with pollution and high crime, clamped to 1-250.
Zones must connect to coal or nuclear plants through power lines or adjacent zones; unpowered zones do not grow and lower the city score.
Tax revenue is collected periodically from population, land value, and tax rate; police, fire, and road funding fractions scale their effects, and underfunded roads decay.
One city-wide tax rate adds a positive offset to demand at low rates and a negative offset at high rates.
Police and fire stations write funding-scaled effect values to a block map that is smoothed outward.
Crime per cell is 128 - land value + density minus smoothed police effect, clamped 0-250.
Industry and traffic write a pollution map that depresses land value and can summon the monster.
Zones generate trips along roads; the resulting traffic density map adds to pollution and complaints.
Map windows show land value, crime, pollution, traffic density, police and fire coverage, and population density.
Fire, flood, tornado, earthquake, and a pollution-gated monster fire at 1/481, 1/241, or 1/61 per cycle by difficulty.
Time-limited scenarios such as Detroit 1972 set a goal to reach before the clock ends, added at Broderbund's suggestion.
A yearly evaluation turns problem scores into a 0-1000 rating and an approval poll.

name: SimCity
summary: The city builder in which a mayor zones residential, commercial, and industrial land, lays power and roads, and sets taxes while grid maps of land value, crime, pollution, and traffic drive where the city grows.

core_loop: shape terrain and zone light or dense residential, commercial, industrial land -> lay power lines, water pipes, roads, and rail -> demand and land value grow zones -> set per-zone tax rates, ordinances, and bonds -> fund schools, hospitals, police, and fire -> rebuild aging plants
design_notes: SimCity 2000 keeps the original's grid-map model but adds a second plane: an underground view for water pipes, subways, and road tunnels, so infrastructure is laid on a separate layer from zoning. Finance gains levers (three tax rates, ordinances, bonds), and most of the nine power plant types have limited lifespans, so replacement becomes a recurring capital cost. Yearly newspapers built from city state replace the score screen, and extreme deficit spending ends the game.

mechanics.note: Residential, commercial, and industrial zones in light and dense variants, plus seaport and airport zones.
Demand bars for residential, commercial, and industrial land, raised by connections to neighbor cities.
Nine plant types including wind, hydro, solar, fusion, and microwave; most have limited lifespans and must be rebuilt.
Yearly budget with department funding; extreme deficit spending ends the game.
Separate tax rates for residential, commercial, and industrial zones.
The player issues bonds to raise capital and pays interest on them.
City ordinances enacted for ongoing cost and effect.
An underground layer holds water pipes, subways, and road tunnels separate from the surface.
Water from pumps travels through underground pipes to zones.
Land has elevation that the player can raise or lower before and during play.
Schools, libraries, museums, hospitals, police, and fire stations cover surrounding zones.
Query tool shows land value per tile, which shapes development.
Query tool reports traffic on roads; highways and transit relieve it.
Disasters strike in play, and scenarios based on real cities stage specific ones.
Power plant types such as solar, fusion, and microwave and buildings such as arcologies become available in set invention years as the city's calendar advances.

name: SimCity 2000
summary: The isometric sequel to SimCity that adds terrain elevation, an underground layer of water pipes and subways, separate zone tax rates, bonds, ordinances, and power plants that age out.

core_loop: zone along roads -> GlassBox agents carry workers, goods, power, water, and sewage between buildings -> specialize the city in industries such as manufacturing, education, or tourism -> trade surpluses and share services with region neighbors -> pool resources into Great Works
design_notes: GlassBox replaces statistical maps with units that hold resource bins and agents that move resources between them, so a house holds a count of people and food, water travels as units, and traffic jams are the visible sum of commuting agents. Agents take the first available job and the first empty home rather than keeping persistent lives, and vehicles take the shortest route instead of the least loaded one, which players read as pathfinding errors. Cities were smaller than earlier games by design, and region play links them asynchronously through shared services, trade, and Great Works.

mechanics.note: Residential, commercial, and industrial zones are painted along roads; buildings develop inside them.
Sims go to the first job and first empty home they find; vehicles take the shortest route rather than the one with spare capacity.
Jams emerge from masses of commuting Sim agents on the road network.
Cities in a region connect by highway, rail, and water, trade resources, share services, and pool wealth into Great Works such as an arcology.
Power is carried as resource units from plants to buildings.
Water and sewage move as units through pipes between pumps, treatment, and buildings.
Map resources are mostly finite, though groundwater recharges.
A simulated global market raises and lowers prices of key resources with supply and demand.
Service buildings dispatch vehicle agents to calls.
Pollution and traffic cross city borders within a region.
Residents and businesses come in wealth levels with different demands.

name: SimCity (2013)
summary: A SimCity reboot built on the agent-based GlassBox engine, in which agents carry workers, power, water, and goods between buildings and small cities share a region over an always-online connection.

core_loop: terraform in God mode -> zone residential, commercial, industrial land at a density and connect roads -> wealth-level demand and desirability grow buildings -> set taxes and per-building service funding -> trade power, water, and garbage with neighbor cities -> grow the region
design_notes: SimCity 4 splits each zone type by wealth level, so demand and desirability are tracked per class and neighborhoods can decay or gentrify as conditions change. Cities of 1 to 4 km per side sit in a region and exchange water, electricity, and garbage disposal through neighbor deals, letting several specialized cities depend on each other; this single-player region has no exact match in the taxonomy (see run proposal). Its commute model drew praise from urban planner Jeff Speck, and the Building Architect Tool (2004) sustained a content community for over two decades.

mechanics.note: Residential, commercial, and industrial zones at low, medium, and high density, with agriculture as a separate industrial zone; buildings need road frontage.
Demand is reported separately for each wealth level of residents and for commercial and industrial subtypes.
Desirability is computed separately for each wealth level, so the same lot attracts different classes as services and nuisances change.
Commuters route trips over roads, rail, and transit; Rush Hour adds traffic flow tracing, avenues, and elevated rail.
Buildings belong to wealth levels and size stages; areas decay or gentrify.
Bus, subway, and rail stations carry commuters; Rush Hour adds elevated rail.
Civic buildings need ongoing funding set per building.
Tax rates per zone type and wealth level.
Schools, hospitals, police, and fire buildings cover areas; they lose output and gain maintenance cost as they age.
City ordinances with monthly costs and effects.
God mode reshapes terrain; most terraforming locks once a city is founded.
God mode triggers disasters on the city.
Mayor mode advisors comment on problems and suggest actions.
Industry and traffic pollute and reduce desirability.

name: SimCity 4
summary: A city builder in which several cities share a region map and trade utilities, while zones develop by density and wealth level and a commute model routes trips across roads and transit.

core_loop: set geological, atmospheric, and biological rates -> climate and biomes evolve -> taxa spread, mutate, and diversify -> one sapient species advances through seven ages -> pollution, war, and disasters feed back on climate -> spend energy on interventions
design_notes: Will Wright and Fred Haslam built SimEarth with James Lovelock as adviser, and its models encode Gaian feedback: volcanic dust cools the planet, warming melts ice caps and raises seas, and life alters atmospheric gas fractions shown to three decimal places. The player mostly acts through control panels that set rates such as continental drift, reproduction, and mutation, plus energy-priced interventions (50 units per terrain square, 500 per terraforming device), so play is closer to tuning coupled systems than to directing agents. Scenarios include Daisyworld, Lovelock's minimal model of temperature regulation by daisy color, and terraforming Mars and Venus.

mechanics.note: Atmospheric composition, temperature, ocean level, and biomes evolve together under Gaian feedback; volcanic dust cools, warming melts ice caps, extreme heat boils oceans, and Daisyworld reduces it to daisies regulating temperature.
Placing terrain, life, monoliths, oxygen generators, and terraforming devices costs energy (50 per terrain square, 500 per device) from a budget that grows with planetary development.

Taxa from prokaryotes to mammals spread and diversify by environment, with player-set reproduction and mutation rates; mass extinctions are often followed by renewed radiation, and any multicellular taxon can become sapient.
Mars, Venus, Ice Planet, and Dune scenarios ask the player to make hostile planets habitable.
Hurricanes, wildfires, earthquakes, tsunamis, and meteors occur, with disease and pollution scaling with population.

name: SimEarth
summary: A planetary god game built on James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis in which geology, atmosphere, climate, life, and civilization models interact over billions of years under the player's parameter changes and interventions.

core_loop: design species genes and world physics -> plants grow and animals eat, breed, and mutate -> populations boom, crash, or go extinct -> read graphs -> edit genes or environment and run again
design_notes: Designed by Ken Karakotsios, SimLife moves the player's control point down to the genome: plant and animal species are edited gene by gene, and the world's physical parameters can be changed, so the toy is about running ecological and evolutionary experiments rather than pursuing goals. Where SimEarth aggregates taxa into planetary stocks, SimLife works at the scale of a landscape and its individual species, mixing exclusive designed animals such as the Killer Penguin and Monkeyphant with player-made ones. Direct gene editing matches the genome-modification proposal from run catalog-ge.

mechanics.note: The player edits the genetics of plant and animal species directly, and offspring inherit those genes with variation.
Evolution is simulated and can be steered; species whose genes fit the designed environment persist while others decline.
Designed ecosystems pair plant species with the animals that eat them, so gene edits ripple through who can feed on whom.
Players create and modify worlds and environments as well as species.

name: SimLife
summary: A Maxis artificial-life toy in which the player edits plant and animal genes, landscape, and the world's physical parameters, then watches food chains and evolution play out.

core_loop: build floors, lobbies, and elevators -> place offices, condos, hotels, and shops -> tenants travel by elevator on daily routines -> long waits raise stress and drive tenants out -> rent and population raise the star rating -> unlock new facilities
design_notes: SimTower turns a building into a vertical transit problem: standard elevators span up to 30 floors and express elevators the full height, so the player designs shafts, sky lobbies, and stops to keep queues short as the tower grows toward 100 floors above ground and 9 below. Tenant stress, not money alone, gates the star rating from one to five and finally the Tower rating, which needs a cathedral on top. Events such as a terrorist bomb ransom, VIP visits that can unlock a star, fires, and pests interrupt the routine.

mechanics.note: Tenants wait at elevator lobbies; long waits raise stress, and stressed tenants move out.
Floors and tenant units are placed on a side-view grid; tenant type and position set elevator demand.
Office workers, residents, shoppers, and hotel guests travel at different times of day, creating rush periods at lobbies.
Population and conditions advance the tower from one to five stars and then to Tower status, each step unlocking facility types.
Up to 100 floors above ground and 9 below; standard elevators span 30 floors, express elevators the full height.
People route between floors by elevators, escalators, and stairs.
Rent and sales income fund construction.
Terrorist bomb threats with a ransom or search, fires, and pest infestations.

name: SimTower
summary: A skyscraper management game in which the player stacks offices, condos, hotels, and shops and designs elevator service so tenants on daily routines do not wait long enough to stress out and leave.

core_loop: take a delivery or repair task -> pick truck, tires, and attachments -> drive into deforming mud, snow, or water -> recover when stuck -> deliver cargo -> earn money and rank -> unlock upgrades and new trucks
design_notes: Terrain is the antagonist: mud, snow, and water respond to vehicle weight, speed, and momentum, so route choice and tire type matter more than speed, and optional timed contests pay more for faster completion. The physics engine is the one Pavel Zagrebelnyy built for MudRunner, the sequel to Spintires. Mechanical upgrades such as snorkels and chain tires are gated behind progress thresholds, and up to four players can share a map.

mechanics.note: Mud, snow, and water react to each truck's weight, speed, and momentum, so ground conditions change as vehicles pass and can bog down underpowered or wrongly fitted trucks.
Tire types, frame attachments, and accessories such as exhaust snorkels for deep water and chain tires for snow change how each of over 60 trucks copes with terrain.
Missions deliver cargo or complete construction and repair jobs; optional timed contests pay more the faster they are finished.
Damage is shown on the vehicle model and in the interface and must be repaired.
Mechanical upgrades require reaching a progress threshold.

name: SnowRunner
summary: An off-road trucking sim in which the player hauls cargo across mud, snow, and water whose surfaces deform under each truck's weight and tires, upgrading a fleet to reach harder terrain.

core_loop: lay out houses, streets, and workshops -> tens of thousands of citizens and slaves work, worship, and seek their desires -> appoint nobles to run the realm -> supply and train armies -> fight real-time battles -> trade, ally, or conquer neighboring kingdoms
design_notes: Songs of Syx scales individual simulation to city size: each of tens of thousands of citizens and slaves has a race, religion, fears, and desires, and each soldier in battles of up to 50,000 units needs supplies. Nobles can be appointed or imported to manage the kingdom but may try to usurp the player. The game has been in early access since September 2020 with no fixed 1.0 date.

mechanics.note: Citizens and slaves of several races, each with distinct needs, religion, and roles.
Real-time battles of up to 50,000 individual units commanded by the player.
Each citizen's needs and desires drive behavior.
Tens of thousands of agents path through streets to work and services.
Every soldier must be supplied.
Alliances, trade, and war with other kingdoms.
Appointed nobles may try to usurp the ruler.

name: Songs of Syx
summary: A low-fantasy city builder in which tens of thousands of individually simulated citizens and slaves of several races live in a growing city-state whose armies of up to 50,000 units fight real-time battles.

core_loop: mine ore from voxel asteroids and planets -> refine and assemble components -> weld blocks into ship or station grids -> power and pilot under inertia -> collide, fight, or deform -> repair and redesign
design_notes: Space Engineers treats a ship as a grid of blocks where each block has mass, inertia, and hit points, and functional blocks (thrusters per direction, gyroscopes, reactors, cockpits) decide whether it can move at all; there is no ship stat sheet apart from the blocks. Collisions and weapons deform or destroy individual blocks, and terrain is editable voxels, so construction, mining, and damage share one physical model. Survival mode adds a refine-assemble production chain and suit oxygen and energy, and an in-game programmable block lets players automate ships with scripts.

mechanics.note: Ships and stations are small or large grids of armor and functional blocks; thrusters only push along their facing, so thrust coverage on each axis, gyroscope count, and power supply decide handling.
Volumetric physics gives every block mass and inertia; ships drift under Newtonian motion with optional inertia dampeners, and gravity generators and planets pull loose objects.
Asteroid and planet voxels can be drilled and carved, and armor blocks deform or break block by block under collisions and weapon fire.
Hand drills and ship drills mine ore from voxel deposits.
Refineries turn ore into ingots and assemblers turn ingots into components for welding.
Conveyor blocks connect inventories so refineries, assemblers, and cargo containers move items automatically, with sorters filtering flow.
Reactors, solar panels, batteries, and hydrogen engines feed every functional block on a grid; unpowered blocks stop.
The programmable block runs player-written C# scripts that read and command blocks on the grid.
Sensors, timer blocks, and event controllers trigger block actions without code.
In survival the suit tracks health, energy, oxygen, and hydrogen.
Air vents pressurize sealed rooms with oxygen; breaches depressurize them.
Grids save as blueprints that a projector block displays for welding and that are shared on Steam Workshop.
A C# modding API, Workshop, and mod.io support custom blocks and logic.
Each block has hit points, and damaged functional blocks such as thrusters, reactors, and gyroscopes stop working until welded back.

name: Space Engineers
summary: A voxel sandbox where players mine asteroids and planets and build ships and stations block by block, with every block carrying mass, inertia, power needs, and damage under Newtonian physics.

core_loop: build the ship tile by tile -> balance oxygen, CO2, temperature, and power -> crew work and meet needs -> jump through hyperspace to a new sector -> mine, salvage derelicts, trade, or fight factions -> grow the ship and crew
design_notes: Bugbyte describes it as combining RimWorld-style emergent storytelling with a tile-based gas simulation, and names RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, Spacebase DF-9, and Oxygen Not Included as inspirations. The ship is both the base and the vehicle, so layout choices (a bed beside the ship core disrupts sleep) and life support are coupled to combat, where fire, smoke, gas, and hull breaches cascade through the same simulation. Early access began in May 2020 and 1.0 shipped in May 2026.

mechanics.note: Each tile holds gas quantities; life support modules produce oxygen and remove CO2, and hazardous gases from facilities, fires, or explosions spread until scrubbed or vented.
Hull, walls, doors, and facilities are placed freely tile by tile to form the ship, which can be expanded or rebuilt at any time.
Crew needs for food, sleep, comfort, safety, and friends drive mood, alongside conditions such as starvation or feeling unhygienic.
Neglected crew suffer mental breaks ranging from starting fights to venting other crew into space.
Thermal regulators keep compartments at comfortable temperatures.
Power nodes distribute electricity across the ship.
Crew relationships added in 2022.
Standing with pirates, slavers, merchants, cults, and android factions.
Asteroids are mined for raw materials.
Raw materials are refined into building materials.
Crew are drafted and equipped for ground combat and away missions.
Fire and smoke spread through damaged compartments.
Each playthrough generates a new galaxy of sectors, stations, and ships.

name: Space Haven
summary: A spaceship colony sim in which the player builds a ship tile by tile and keeps a crew with needs, moods, and relationships alive inside a tile-based simulation of oxygen, CO2, heat, and power.

claims.text: Barth's earlier Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering (2008), which is not in this dataset, is the documented precursor of SpaceChem's manipulator puzzles.

core_loop: read the input and output molecules -> place waldo paths and instruction icons in a 10x8 reactor -> run and debug collisions -> meet the output quota -> compare cycles, reactors, and instructions on histograms -> optimize or move on
design_notes: SpaceChem made the program itself the factory: each 10x8 reactor holds two waldos, red and blue, programmed independently or synchronized by instruction icons laid on the grid, and multiple reactors connect on a planet-surface pipeline so one reactor's output feeds another. Execution is deterministic, so a solution either produces the quota or deadlocks or collides, and success is followed by global histograms of cycles, reactors, and instructions that Zach Barth designed to show where a solution sits without the intimidation of a ranked leaderboard. Each planet ends in a defense level where production must keep pace with an attacker. Barth expanded the manipulator puzzles of his 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering, and the instruction-grid plus histogram template recurs across Zachtronics' later games. ResearchNet let players share puzzles.

mechanics.note: Two waldos per reactor, red and blue, follow player-placed paths and instruction icons that pick up, rotate, drop, bond, and route atoms, programmed independently or synchronized, with deterministic and visible execution.
A solution passes when it outputs the required molecule quota and is then scored on cycles, number of reactors, and number of instructions used.
After completion the player's cycles, reactors, and instructions are plotted on global histograms of other players' solutions, chosen over a ranked leaderboard to avoid discouraging players.

Reactors placed on a larger planet map pass molecules through pipelines, so later puzzles split a synthesis across several reactors, some limited to tasks such as breaking bonds, with fission and fusion nodes.
Each puzzle fixes inputs, target outputs, available reactor types, and quotas; defense levels add a time pressure from an attacking enemy.
ResearchNet distributes user-made puzzles that other players download and solve.

name: SpaceChem
summary: A programming puzzle game in which the player lays out instruction paths for two waldos in grid reactors that grab, bond, rotate, and split atoms into target molecules, with each solution scored on cycles, reactors, and instructions against global histograms.

claims.text: The free Proof of Concept Demo Alpha 0.4.0 was publicly released on 2012-05-27, and the game entered Steam Early Access on 2018-09-28 without a later 1.0 release.
The developer is credited only by the handle Quasar on Steam and the development blog; no personal name was found in the sources checked.

core_loop: creatures feed, pay energy costs, and reproduce -> offspring genomes mutate -> environment and rovers decide who eats and who starves -> trait averages drift and lineages split into species -> player edits genes, climate, or triggers ice ages and floods -> watch the clade diagram branch
design_notes: Species, built by a single developer known as Quasar, simulates evolution with no fitness function: genes are numbers, most mutations add a random value in [-1, 1] scaled by a background mutation rate and radiation, and survival is whatever the body and environment allow. Energy costs come from analyzing each creature's skeleton for internal forces and torques, so morphology has a physical price, and creatures can eat only what their head reaches. Species are not predefined: a species is a population that can interbreed within a genetic distance, and it splits only when intermediate forms die out, which the clade diagram records. Species defined at runtime by genetic distance are not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal runtime-speciation). A free alpha (0.4.0) was public from 2012, and the Steam Early Access build from 2018 has not reached 1.0.

mechanics.note: Each creature's body and behavior come from numeric genes; offspring are randomly modified copies of one or more parents, with most mutations a random value in [-1, 1] times a modifier for background mutation rate and radiation.
No fitness score exists; creatures that cannot pay skeleton-derived energy costs, reach food, or tolerate local climate fail to reproduce, so trait averages drift and lineages speciate.
Climate varies across the map, and climate control devices create local cold, hot, fertile, or dead ground.
The player triggers ice ages and world floods, programs rovers to feed or kill creatures by genetic distance to a target genome, and edits genomes in an isolated nursery.
Creature inspection shows each individual's DNA and stats.
Species averages over time, a clade diagram (Tree of Life), a satellite range map, and a web-of-life view of genetic variety.

name: Species: Artificial Life, Real Evolution
summary: A solo-developed evolution simulator in which creatures defined by numeric genes mutate, breed, and speciate in real time across a 3D world while the player observes, edits the gene pool, and alters climate.

core_loop: eat to earn DNA points -> edit body parts to change abilities -> befriend or fight other species -> stage completes and grants consequence traits -> next stage changes the rules -> colonize and terraform planets -> creations upload to the Sporepedia and populate other players' galaxies
design_notes: Spore's evolution is player design rather than selection: body parts bought with DNA points set speed, attack, and social abilities directly, and nothing is inherited by differential survival. Its distinctive system is the part-based editors (18 share one interface) whose creations are stored as compact descriptions of a few kilobytes and reconstructed procedurally, which let Maxis upload every creation and redistribute them as the inhabitants of other players' galaxies (over 100 million by May 2009). Each of the five stages swaps in a different genre's rules, and play style in each stage assigns consequence traits that carry forward.

mechanics.note: Creature, building, and vehicle editors assemble parts such as mouths, legs, and arms whose choice sets abilities, diet options, and stats; textures and animation are applied procedurally to the assembled topology.
Every creation uploads automatically to the Sporepedia and is redistributed to populate other players' worlds, so other players' designs fill the galaxy without manual import.

Each stage ends at a progress threshold and hands the species to a new rule set (cell, creature, tribal, civilization, space), with three consequence traits awarded from how aggressive or social the player was.
The player directly steers the cell, the creature, and later a spaceship.
Tribal and civilization stages switch to commanding up to 12 tribe members, then vehicles and cities.
Creature-stage species, tribes, nations, and space empires such as the Grox can be befriended through social actions or conquered.
In the space stage rocky planets can be terraformed, their ecosystems changed, and features such as mountains and lakes added.

name: Spore
summary: A five-stage game in which the player guides a species from cell to galactic empire, building its body, vehicles, and buildings in part-based editors whose creations are shared automatically through the Sporepedia.

core_loop: plan the day -> spend energy watering, harvesting, mining, or fishing -> sell crops and artisan goods -> buy seeds, tools, and buildings -> gift and talk to villagers -> complete Community Center bundles -> new areas and seasons open
design_notes: Eric Barone built Stardew Valley alone over about five years in response to Harvest Moon, keeping its seasonal crop calendar and town relationships while leaving the long-term structure open-ended. Each day is bounded by an energy bar refilled each morning and a clock that forces sleep, so play is a daily allocation problem across farming, foraging, fishing, mining, and socializing. Friendship is a point stock (250 points per heart, 10 hearts for most villagers) that loses 2 points per day without conversation and accepts two gifts per week, with birthday gifts worth eight times as much. Community Center bundles make collection the main progression gate.

mechanics.note: Seasonal seeds need daily watering (rain or sprinklers substitute) and grow through stages over set day counts; most crops must be harvested before the season changes.
Four 28-day seasons gate which crops grow, which fish and forage appear, and which festivals occur.
An energy bar refills each morning, drains with tool use, and is restored by food; the clock forces bed by 2 a.m. or the player passes out and loses money.

Each villager has a friendship stock of 250 points per heart up to 10 hearts; it decays 2 points per day without talking, takes two gifts a week, multiplies birthday gifts by 8, and unlocks heart events.
Community Center bundles ask for sets of crops, forage, fish, and artisan goods; completed rooms repair town infrastructure and unlock areas, and the museum collects minerals and artifacts.
Barns and coops house animals that produce eggs, milk, and wool when fed and cared for; animals cannot be slaughtered.
Twelve marriage candidates regardless of player gender; spouses help with chores, and couples can have children.
Farming, foraging, fishing, mining, and combat levels rise with practice and unlock recipes and professions.
Kegs, preserves jars, and other machines convert crops and animal products into higher-value artisan goods over fixed processing times.
Crops and animal products come in normal, silver, gold, and iridium quality.
A help-wanted board posts item, fishing, and slaying requests from townspeople.
Recipes turn gathered materials into sprinklers, fences, machines, and bombs.
Villagers follow routines that vary by weekday, season, and weather.
Rain waters crops and changes fish and villager routines.

name: Stardew Valley
summary: A farming and life sim in which the player restores an inherited farm over four 28-day seasons, splitting a daily energy budget among crops, animals, mining, fishing, and friendships with Pelican Town's residents.

core_loop: land with a starter kit -> mine and smelt ore -> build an airtight frame -> pipe, filter, and heat a breathable atmosphere -> power and automate with logic chips -> expand while fixing pressure, fire, and temperature failures
design_notes: The atmosphere is the main simulated system: each sealed volume and pipe network carries a mix of gases with temperature and pressure, so heating a room raises its pressure, mixing fuel and oxygen can burn or explode, and a pressure difference across a wall can blow it out. Survival needs are deliberately front-loaded; later play is building plant that keeps the atmosphere stable, then automating it with IC10 chips programmed in an assembly language. The game has been in early access since 2017.

mechanics.note: Rooms and pipe networks hold mixtures of oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, volatiles, pollutants, and water with pressure and temperature; gases mix, and combustion consumes fuel and oxygen and releases heat.
Gas temperature changes pressure and habitability; radiators, heat exchangers, heaters, and coolers move heat between pipes, rooms, and the planet's atmosphere.
Pipes, pumps, filtration units, mixers, and regulators route gases between devices; pipes and tanks fail when pressure exceeds their rating.
Early survival requires breathable gas, food, water, and suit temperature; suits carry tanks and filters until a habitat is sealed.
Solar panels, generators, and batteries feed cable networks; overloaded cables burn out.
IC10 chips run player-written assembly that reads and writes device logic values such as pressure and temperature.
Logic readers, writers, memory, and sensors chain devices without code.
Ore is mined from deformable voxel terrain.
Furnaces and arc furnaces smelt ore into ingots, and autolathes and other fabricators turn ingots into kits.
Hydroponic plants need light, water, and suitable gases, and exchange carbon dioxide for oxygen.
Walls hold limited pressure differences; exceeding them causes fatigue and explosive decompression.
Frames, walls, pipes, and devices are placed on a grid piece by piece, and placement decides airtightness.

name: Stationeers
summary: A first-person space station survival game whose core is an atmospheric simulation of gas mixtures, pressure, temperature, and combustion that the player must engineer with pipes, power, and programmable logic.

core_loop: survey systems with science ships -> claim systems and colonize planets -> build districts that create jobs for pops -> draw research cards and build fleets -> negotiate or fight neighboring empires -> survive the late-game crisis
design_notes: Stellaris combines a space 4X opening (survey, claim, colonize) with Paradox grand strategy systems: real time with pause, internal factions, and event chains. Its research model replaces a visible tree with weighted random card draws, so two runs of the same empire research in different orders. Hyperlane-only travel turns the galaxy into a graph with chokepoints. Henrik Fahraeus named Star Control II, Master of Orion II, and Europa Universalis IV as roughly equal influences.

mechanics.note: Physics, society, and engineering research each offer three semi-random project cards weighted by ethics, the scientist's traits, and known technologies; rare technologies and anomaly-granted cards vary each run, and costs rise as the game goes on.

Pops fill jobs created by planetary districts and buildings in worker, specialist, and ruler strata; each job consumes and produces resources such as energy, minerals, food, consumer goods, and alloys.
Anomalies found by science ships open authored event chains, and galactic crises such as marauder invasions, awakened machine empires, and extradimensional invaders begin after set periods.
Empires negotiate, form federations, and go to war; ethics such as xenophobe or xenophile shape AI attitudes.
Pops join political factions according to ethics, and faction support produces unity.
Planets beyond the core limit can be grouped into sectors run by AI governors with a player-set focus.
Ships are designed from hull sections and components.
Each galaxy is generated with star systems linked only by hyperlanes.
Species traits and leader traits modify output and behavior.
Ethics, civics, policies, and edicts change empire rules.
Unity, produced partly by faction support, buys traditions, and influence pays for new outposts and territorial claims.
Empire size grows with systems, colonies, and pops, and size beyond administrative capacity raises technology and tradition costs; bureaucrat jobs add capacity to offset it.
Each pop holds an ethic that drifts toward ethics with higher attraction, modified by government ethics, policies, and living conditions, and pop ethics decide faction membership.
Empires take systems by building outposts, borders follow owned systems, and claims bought with influence set what wars can take.
War exhaustion rises from losses and occupation, and a side at maximum exhaustion can be forced into a status quo peace.
Fleet battles resolve from ship weapons, shields, armor, and hull values against each other, and ground combat compares army attack and health.

name: Stellaris
summary: A real-time-with-pause space 4X and grand strategy game in which the player designs a species and empire, expands across a procedurally generated hyperlane galaxy from 2200, manages pops, jobs, ethics-based factions, and research card draws, and faces late-game crises.

core_loop: dive from the lifepod -> gather resources and recover blueprints -> craft tools, vehicles, and base modules -> manage oxygen, food, and water -> dive deeper into new biomes and story sites -> build the means to escape the planet
design_notes: Included as a boundary case: the map, story, and progression are hand-authored, and the simulated layer is a set of survival meters plus base power and fauna behavior. Oxygen is the distinctive meter because it ties survival to depth and distance from air, making range a resource. Mode settings remove meters to change genre: Freedom drops hunger and thirst, Creative drops all depleting stats, and Hardcore adds permanent death without low-oxygen warnings.

mechanics.note: Health, hunger, thirst, and oxygen deplete in Survival mode; oxygen limits each dive's depth and duration, Freedom mode removes hunger and thirst, and Creative removes all depleting stats.
Gathered resources are crafted into tools, base parts, and submersibles from blueprints the player has recovered.
Bases are assembled from placed modules.
Bases and vehicles need energy sources.
A day-night cycle and frequent eclipses change visibility.
Cooked fish spoils over time; cured fish does not.
Optional in Hardcore mode.

name: Subnautica
summary: An underwater survival game on an ocean planet where the player manages oxygen, food, and water while crafting tools, submersibles, and bases to explore deeper and escape.

claims.text: Suck Up! was publicly playable through Proxima's own launcher before its Steam 1.0 release on 2025-10-01; the site's terms, last updated 2023-12-05, already metered AI-model use in tokens, and the site calls the launcher build early access.

core_loop: pick a disguise -> knock on a resident's door -> speak a pitch aloud -> the model replies in character and weighs trust -> get invited in and feed, or get refused -> next house
design_notes: At runtime a language model plays each resident: the player's spoken words go to a hosted model (the Steam page lists ChatGPT from OpenAI; the December 2023 terms name GPT 3.5 and Llama 2 and meter use in tokens) along with the resident's authored personality, and its reply, delivered in voiced audio, decides whether the player has earned entry. The challenge is social engineering against a model that has been told to be suspicious, so disguises (knight, superhero, a previous victim) work as context that changes the model's judgment. Players author new residents' personalities and whole neighborhoods and share them on Steam Workshop. It is a boundary case: the persuasion is judged by the model rather than by a simulated social state.

mechanics.note: The player talks to residents with a real microphone, and the store page says responses depend on tone and strategy.
A hosted language model (ChatGPT from OpenAI per the store page) generates each resident's reply and in-character decision in real time from its personality prompt and the conversation.
Each resident has an authored personality and behaviors that condition the model, and players can write their own.
Steam Workshop shares player-made characters and full neighborhoods.
Modes include Love Bites (split up couples at a Valentine's Day party) and Mic Drop (rap battles against characters).

name: Suck Up!
summary: A voice-controlled comedy game in which the player, as a disguised vampire, talks AI-driven townspeople into letting them inside, with each resident's replies generated by a language model from its personality and the player's words.

core_loop: pick a procedure -> move the hand and press finger keys to grab tools -> cut, break, and remove body parts -> place the new organ -> keep Bob alive -> score and time
design_notes: Made in 48 hours at the 2013 Global Game Jam, the game turns control difficulty into the content: the mouse moves the hand, a mouse button rotates or lowers it, and A, W, E, R, and Space close individual fingers, a scheme modeled on Jurassic Park: Trespasser. Tools and organs are rigid bodies, so most outcomes come from collisions and dropped objects rather than authored surgical steps. Medicine is a comic frame with a thin vital-sign model; a heart rate at zero requires charging the defibrillators. Included as a boundary case for embodied control.

mechanics.note: The mouse moves the hand, holding the right button rotates it, the left button lowers it, and A, W, E, R, and Space each close one finger, so grasping a scalpel is itself the challenge.
Instruments, organs, and bones are physics objects that collide, slip, and fall, so most mistakes are physical accidents rather than authored failure states.
Damage to the patient drives a small vital-sign model; when heart rate reaches 0 the player must charge the defibrillators.
Procedures such as heart and kidney transplants are replayed in an operating room, a bouncing ambulance, and zero gravity.

name: Surgeon Simulator
summary: A physics comedy surgery game in which the player controls one hand with separate finger keys to perform transplants on the patient Bob before his vital signs fail.

core_loop: land rockets with drones and prefabs -> drones build power, water, and oxygen infrastructure -> build domes and bring colonists from Earth -> colonists' traits, comfort, and sanity drive work and stability -> research and export rare metals for funding -> weather disasters and Mysteries
design_notes: Surviving Mars splits construction from population: drones working within range of hubs build and maintain everything, and colonists arrive only after domes have power, water, and oxygen. Colonists carry traits, flaws, and specializations and track morale, comfort, sanity, and health, so dome services decide whether they work, turn Earthsick, or rebel. Mysteries layer authored storylines (plagues, rival corporations, AI revolts, alien contact) on top of disasters such as dust storms, meteors, and cold waves.

mechanics.note: Generators and batteries feed cable networks to domes and buildings; a dome without power, water, or oxygen cannot sustain colonists.
Water and oxygen travel by pipe from extractors and producers to domes.
Drones within a hub's range carry resources, build, and maintain buildings.
Research spans physics, engineering, social, biotechnology, and robotics fields.
Drone hubs and dome services serve within a range.
Colonists have traits, flaws, and specializations that suit them to jobs.
Comfort, sanity, health, and morale change with services and events.
Unhappy colonists may become Earthsick or rebels.
Dust storms, meteor storms, cold waves, and dust devils.
Buildings need drone maintenance to keep working.
Green Planet (2019) adds terraforming of atmosphere, temperature, and water.
Mysteries run storylines such as plagues, rival corporations, AI revolts, and alien contact.
Metals, rare metals, concrete, and water are extracted; rare metal exports fund imports.

name: Surviving Mars
summary: A Mars colony city builder in which drones build power, water, and oxygen networks before colonists with traits arrive in domes, while research, Earth sponsors, and dust storms, meteors, and cold waves shape survival.

core_loop: read briefings and dialogue -> choose responses and policy decisions -> budget, alignment, and story flags update -> later options open or close -> reach an ending and a political-compass result
design_notes: Suzerain is mostly authored text, about 450,000 words, in which choices are recorded as state: the budget and accumulated decisions gate later dialogue options and endings. It is a boundary case included for how a political game can run on dilemma choices and state-gated story branches rather than an equation network. The ending screen places the player on an in-universe political compass computed from choices made across the term.

mechanics.note: Ministers, advisers, and family members present situations as dialogue, and multiple-choice responses on constitutional reform, economic model, security, and welfare trade off budget, alignment, and later options.
Story chapters branch on recorded choices, opening or closing later scenes and deciding which ending the term reaches.
Available budget and resources are shown and drawn down by decisions.
Sordland can side with the western or eastern bloc or stay neutral, and deals with its neighbor Rumburg.
Major choices set constitutional reforms and a market-driven or centrally planned economy.
Ministers and advisers brief the president and argue positions.

name: Suzerain
summary: A text-based political narrative game in which the player, as newly elected President Anton Rayne of Sordland, makes dialogue and policy choices across one term that shift the budget, foreign alignment, and constitutional reform toward one of several endings.

core_loop: pet calls for attention -> feed a meal or snack, play, scold, clean, or give medicine -> meters and care history accumulate -> pet ages after each sleep -> care history selects its next form -> it lives on or dies
design_notes: Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi reduced a pet to three meters (Hunger, Happy, Training) plus droppings and sickness on a three-button LCD device that runs continuously; early units could pause only through the clock settings. Meals fill Hunger, snacks and a minigame raise Happy but excess snacks cause illness, scolding when the pet calls for attention fills Training, and uncleaned droppings lead to sickness shown by a skull. Each life stage lasts a set number of days and age advances when the pet wakes, and care quality selects the adult character, turning care history into a visible outcome (proposed as care-dependent-development).

mechanics.note: Care actions are meal, snack, game, scold, clean, and medicine; meals are limited by fullness while snacks are not, and excess snacks cause sickness.
Hunger and Happy meters, shown as hearts, deplete over real time and are refilled by meals, snacks, and the minigame.
The pet lives on the device clock set at hatching and sleeps nightly; time keeps passing between check-ins.
Baby, Child, Teenager, Adult, and Special stages (plus Senior in some models) each last a set number of days, with age advancing on waking; old age eventually ends its life.
Poor care, sickness, or old age kills the pet; the A and C buttons start a new egg.
A nightly sleep period suspends care demands and marks age increments.
The device beeps and shows an attention icon when the pet needs care or calls for discipline.
Care quality during each life stage, such as unanswered calls, overfeeding snacks, and uncleaned droppings, selects the next form, so the same egg can grow into different adult characters.

name: Tamagotchi
summary: A 1996 keychain virtual pet whose hunger, happiness, and training meters run on a real-time clock, and whose care quality determines which adult form it grows into and how long it lives.

core_loop: survey the level -> cut, blast, and ram a route through voxel structures -> stage vehicles and ramps -> trigger the alarm by taking a target -> grab the rest along the planned path before the timer ends
design_notes: Every object is made of small voxels with material types (wood, plaster, brick, metal, glass), and disconnected chunks become rigid bodies that fall, roll, and burn, so geometry is a resource the player spends. The design separates an unlimited planning phase from a timed execution phase: picking up a connected target starts a 60-second alarm, so the player engineers shortcuts with tools, explosives, and vehicles before the first grab. Materials resist tools differently, and fire spreads through wood, which turns construction knowledge into route planning.

mechanics.note: Levels are made of small voxels whose material sets which tools can break them; the sledgehammer breaks soft materials, the blowtorch cuts metal, and explosives remove volumes.
Voxel chunks cut loose become dynamic bodies with mass that fall, roll, and crush; vehicles and cranes push and lift them.
In most heists taking an alarmed target starts a 60-second timer to reach the getaway vehicle, so the route must be prepared during an unlimited setup phase.
Fire spreads across wood and other flammables and can burn targets or open routes; burning structures weaken and fall.
Materials respond differently to each tool and to fire; a fire extinguisher puts fires out.
Sections cut off from all supports fall, so removing pillars can drop a floor.
40 campaign missions specify targets, optional targets, and conditions such as stealing, destroying, or collecting evidence.
Lua scripting, a level editor, and Steam Workshop support custom levels, tools, and modes.

name: Teardown
summary: A heist and destruction game set in fully destructible voxel levels where the player plans a route by cutting, smashing, and driving through structures, then races a 60-second alarm timer to grab the targets.

core_loop: place wind turbines on rock -> power toxin scrubbers that clean soil -> irrigate and pump water into riverbeds -> upgrade to grow wetlands, meadows, and forest -> attract animals and restore weather -> recycle every building and leave
design_notes: It inverts the city-builder loop: growth is measured in restored tiles rather than population, and points earned per restored tile are the only currency for further buildings, so efficient placement compounds. The final step requires recycling all infrastructure to build an airship and leave, so a layout must be removable as well as productive.
